entries.meaning: Points at one person whose identity is unknown to the speaker, irrelevant to the point, or deliberately withheld. It asserts that such a person exists, which is precisely what its polarity partner anybody does not do: somebody called reports a call, did anybody call asks whether one happened at all.
examples: Somebody is knocking at the back door.
We need somebody to sign for the delivery before five.
She's seeing somebody from her old firm.
Somebody's car is blocking the driveway again.
Could somebody please turn the thermostat down? — a request, so some- survives inside a question
There's somebody new in accounting, and I've already forgotten their name. — singular verb, plural-form pronoun, both standard
He said somebody had complained, but he wouldn't say who.
entries.pronunciation note: stress is fixed on some- and never moves; the second element is unstressed, so the vowel centers and the /d/ becomes a tap between vowels, giving the everyday [ˈsʌmbəɾi] — roughly SUM-buh-dee. Many Americans have [ˈsʌmbʌdi]. The full [ˈsʌmˌbɑdi] is citation form and sounds deliberate in running speech
entries.русский: кто-то, кто-нибудь — неназванное лицо; разговорнее, чем someone, глагол всегда в ед. ч.
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; genitive somebody's
entries.register: neutral; a shade more conversational than someone
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun (assertive)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no plural and no gender. The homograph in he's a somebody is a countable noun, not this pronoun, and it does pluralize (nobodies and somebodies).
entries.refers to: an unidentified or unspecified person — human referents only, one at a time. For a thing use something. Animals go with something unless the speaker is treating the animal as a person, which is why somebody chewed my shoe is perfectly natural about a dog.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — Somebody is at the door, Somebody has been in here. The pronoun that refers back is normally singular they/them/their (Somebody left their badge on the table), which is standard American English in edited prose as well as speech; the formal alternative is his or her, and generic he now reads as an error to most American editors.
entries.pattern: somebody [singular verb] · [verb] somebody · [preposition] somebody · somebody's [noun] · somebody [adjective] — the adjective follows (somebody new) · somebody else / somebody else's [noun] · somebody who/that [clause] · somebody to [verb]
entries.contrast: Somebody and someone mean exactly the same thing and swap freely; the only difference is texture, with the -one forms dominant in edited American prose and the -body forms holding their own in speech. Against anybody the difference is polarity: some- in plain affirmative statements, any- under a negative, a question, or an if. The standing exception is the offer or request, which keeps some- inside a question — Could somebody hold the door? invites help, while Could anybody hold the door? sounds like a genuine survey of who is able. Keep the pronoun apart from the noun: he's a somebody now has an article and a plural, which the pronoun never takes.
entries.see also: someone, something, anybody, nobody, somebody else, somebody else's

entries.meaning: Names one person without identifying them. Someone is the written default of the four some- people-words and carries no implication about how many such people exist — only that at least one does.
examples: Someone has been reading my mail.
I'd like someone with actual field experience on the call.
The letter was addressed to someone named A. Reyes.
Someone's phone kept buzzing all through the ceremony.
Is there someone who can cover the front desk until noon? — an appeal for help, so some- is natural in the question
We hired someone new, and they start Monday.
It has to be someone on the inside.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on some-; the -one is unstressed and its vowel routinely centers to /ə/, giving [ˈsʌmwən]. Never stress the second element — a stressed some ONE is the two-word phrase some one (of them), which is a different structure with a different meaning
entries.русский: кто-то, кто-нибудь — неназванное лицо; нейтральный вариант somebody для письменной речи
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; genitive someone's
entries.register: neutral; the unmarked choice in edited writing
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun (assertive)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no plural and no gender.
entries.refers to: an unidentified or unspecified person — human referents only. For a thing use something; for a place use somewhere.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — Someone is waiting, Someone was here before us. Back-reference is singular they/them/their in ordinary American usage (Someone forgot their umbrella); his or her is the conservative formal option and is clumsy when repeated.
entries.pattern: someone [singular verb] · [verb] someone · [preposition] someone · someone's [noun] · someone [adjective] (someone important) · someone else / someone else's [noun] · someone who/that [clause] · someone to [verb]
entries.contrast: The trap is the space bar. Welded into one word, someone is a pronoun meaning a person; split into two, some one is the determiner some plus the pronoun one, it means one particular member of a set already named, and it takes of — some one of the trustees must countersign. That two-word form is stiff and rare now, but its siblings are alive and are the real hazard: every one of the windows and any one of the applicants are two words, and writing ✗ everyone of the windows was cracked is one of the most common errors in this whole family. Against somebody it is free choice, someone being slightly more formal. Against anyone it is polarity: some- asserts, any- questions or denies.
entries.see also: somebody, something, anyone, no one, someone else, someone else's

entries.meaning: Points at an unidentified or unspecified thing. It has three uses that are worth separating.
examples: Something is wrong with the transmission. — sense 1
Grab something to eat before the meeting starts. — sense 1, an infinitive postmodifier
She said something strange and then changed the subject. — sense 1, the adjective following
There's something about the way he tells that story. — sense 2
That last set was really something. — sense 2, predicative
Something like four hundred people showed up. — sense 3
We ordered something off the specials board and regretted it.

senses.head: An unspecified object, idea, event, or substance
body: The core sense, and the one that takes postmodifiers: something wrong, something to eat, something I've been meaning to ask.

senses.head: An unspecified quality or worth
body: There's something about that room. Predicatively it becomes a compliment: That performance was really something.

senses.head: An approximator
body: Before a number it hedges the count — something like two hundred people — and hyphenated after one it makes an age bracket: a thirty-something in a very expensive coat.
examples: Something is wrong with the transmission. — sense 1
Grab something to eat before the meeting starts. — sense 1, an infinitive postmodifier
She said something strange and then changed the subject. — sense 1, the adjective following
There's something about the way he tells that story. — sense 2
That last set was really something. — sense 2, predicative
Something like four hundred people showed up. — sense 3
We ordered something off the specials board and regretted it.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on some-. An epenthetic /p/ appears between the /m/ and the /θ/ in ordinary speech, giving [ˈsʌmpθɪŋ], and casual American English reduces the whole word to [ˈsʌmpm̩] or [ˈsʌmθɪn] — the sump'm and somethin' a learner actually hears. The final /ŋ/ is not /ŋɡ/
entries.русский: что-то, что-нибудь — неназванный предмет, мысль или событие; о людях не говорят
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; a genitive something's is possible but rare and usually rewritten
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun (assertive)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no plural, no gender.
entries.refers to: things, ideas, events, situations, substances, and actions — non-human referents. It reaches a person only in the fixed predicates he's really something and she's something else, where it means remarkable. Back-reference is it, not they: Something arrived; it was in a crate.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — Something is burning, Something has to give, Something smells wrong in here. A following adjective does not change this: Something odd is going on.
entries.pattern: something [singular verb] · [verb] something · [preposition] something · something [adjective] — the adjective follows the pronoun · something to [verb] · something that [clause] · something else · something like [number] (approximation)
entries.contrast: Modifiers follow, they do not precede: ✓ something strange, ✗ strange something. This is the one syntactic quirk shared by all twelve compounds, and it holds for adjectives, prepositional phrases, relative clauses, and infinitives alike (something cheap from the deli that I can microwave). Against anything the rule is polarity, with a scope wrinkle worth knowing: I didn't hear anything denies the whole set, while I didn't hear something is only usable when something sits outside the negation (There's something I didn't hear). Against some thing written as two words, which is the determiner some plus a literal noun and needs a context that makes thing mean an object. Against nothing, its negative counterpart. The hedge something of a genius is a different construction entirely; see something of a.
entries.see also: somebody, someone, anything, nothing, everything, something else, something or other

entries.meaning: Marks a referent as real but unrecoverable: the speaker knows a specific thing is involved and admits to having lost its identity. It is a confession of vagueness rather than genuine indefiniteness, which is why it sounds dismissive when used about someone's work.
examples: He's writing a dissertation on medieval land tenure or something or other.
She left a message about a permit or something or other.
Somebody or other from the county called about the fence line.
I signed something or other at the front desk and never saw it again.
They moved to somewhere or other in Arizona and stopped answering email.
Something or other keeps tripping the breaker in the basement.
entries.pronunciation note: or is always weak, reduced to a syllabic /ɚ/ with no vowel of its own, so the phrase runs as four beats with main stress on oth-; in fast speech the whole thing compresses to [ˈsʌmpm̩ ɚ ˈʌðɚ]
entries.русский: что-то там, что-то такое — разг., когда говорящий не помнит или не хочет уточнять
entries.case: none — invariant; a genitive is not formed on the phrase
entries.register: informal, conversational; a copy editor deletes it or replaces it with a fact
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun with a vagueness tag
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant.
entries.refers to: a thing whose identity the speaker cannot recall or does not care to supply. The parallel forms somebody or other and someone or other refer to people, and somewhere or other to places.
entries.agreement: singular verb — Something or other has gone wrong with the billing again.
entries.pattern: something or other [singular verb] · [verb] something or other · [noun] or something or other (tacked onto a list) · somebody / someone / somewhere or other (the parallel forms)
entries.contrast: The tag attaches only to the some- forms. ✗ anything or other, ✗ nothing or other, ✗ everything or other are all impossible, because the tag's job is to assert that a particular thing exists while confessing ignorance of which one — and only some- makes that assertion. Compare the looser clause-final tag or something (He's a consultant or something), which does the same work with less commitment, and what have you, which closes a list rather than replacing a single item.
entries.variants: somebody or other, someone or other, somewhere or other, someplace or other, somehow or other, sometime or other, some way or other — the tag attaches to any some- form, the adverbs included, and to no other stem
entries.see also: something, somebody, somewhere, whatnot, so-and-so, whatchamacallit, thingamajig, whatsit, God knows what, God knows who

entries.meaning: Refers to a person without asserting that any such person exists. It has two clearly separate lives.
examples: I didn't tell anybody about the offer. — sense 1, under a negative
Has anybody seen my keys? — sense 1, in a question
If anybody asks, we left at nine. — sense 1, in a conditional
Anybody can learn to solder with an afternoon of practice. — sense 2, free choice
Hardly anybody stayed for the second half.
She works harder than anybody else in that department. — the comparative frame; else because she works there too
Nobody told me — not ✗ anybody didn't tell me.

senses.head: Nonassertive
body: Under a negative, a question, or a condition, it simply widens the search to the whole class: I didn't see anybody denies every candidate, one by one.

senses.head: Free choice
body: In an affirmative clause, usually with a modal, it means it does not matter which and carries its own stress: Anybody can learn to solder. This is the sense that lets any- appear where the polarity rule would otherwise forbid it.
examples: I didn't tell anybody about the offer. — sense 1, under a negative
Has anybody seen my keys? — sense 1, in a question
If anybody asks, we left at nine. — sense 1, in a conditional
Anybody can learn to solder with an afternoon of practice. — sense 2, free choice
Hardly anybody stayed for the second half.
She works harder than anybody else in that department. — the comparative frame; else because she works there too
Nobody told me — not ✗ anybody didn't tell me.

entries.pronunciation note: any is /ˈɛni/ in General American — the vowel is that of pen, never that of pan. The /d/ taps between vowels, so the everyday form is [ˈɛnibəɾi]. In the free-choice sense the stress shifts forward and strengthens: ANYbody can do it
entries.русский: кто-нибудь (в вопросе и отрицании); любой, кто угодно (в утверждении)
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; genitive anybody's
entries.register: neutral; a shade more conversational than anyone
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun (nonassertive and free choice)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no plural, no gender.
entries.refers to: a person, human referents only, with no commitment as to which one or whether one exists at all. For things use anything.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always, including in the free-choice sense where the meaning is emphatically universal — Anybody is welcome to try, Has anybody seen my keys?, If anybody calls, take a message. Back-reference is singular they: If anybody objects, ask them to put it in writing.
entries.pattern: [negated verb] anybody (I didn't tell anybody) · Did / has / can [subject] [verb] anybody (question) · if / unless [subject] [verb] anybody (conditional) · hardly / rarely / never / without … anybody · [comparative] than anybody · anybody [singular verb] (free choice: anybody can join) · anybody's [noun] · anybody else / anybody else's
entries.contrast: Two rules, and the second is the one learners miss. Polarity: any- belongs under a negative, in a question, in an if-clause, after hardly / rarely / never / without / before, and after a comparative; some- belongs in plain statements. Order: an any- compound must come after the negative that licenses it, never before it. ✓ I didn't tell anybody, ✗ Anybody didn't tell me — the subject slot in front of a negated verb takes nobody instead (Nobody told me). Against nobody, the pair not … anybody and nobody mean the same thing, with nobody the more emphatic and the only one available at the front of a clause. Against somebody, remember the offer exception runs the other way: a question that is really an invitation keeps some-.
entries.see also: anyone, anything, anybody else, anyone else, somebody, nobody, everybody, any

entries.meaning: Refers to a person while leaving open both who and whether. Like anybody it splits into a nonassertive use and a free-choice use.
examples: Did anyone call while I was out? — sense 1
I don't know anyone who has actually read the whole report. — sense 1
If anyone has a conflict, say so now. — sense 1
Anyone is welcome to sit in on the rehearsal. — sense 2
She is faster over ten kilometers than anyone else on the team. — the comparative frame; else because she is on the team herself
Anyone who wants a copy should send me their address. — singular verb, singular they
It is anyone's guess how long the funding lasts.

senses.head: Nonassertive
body: In negatives, questions, and conditionals it sweeps the whole class without claiming a member exists: Did anyone call?

senses.head: Free choice
body: In affirmative clauses, usually with can, may, or a generic present, it means no matter who: Anyone is welcome to sit in.
examples: Did anyone call while I was out? — sense 1
I don't know anyone who has actually read the whole report. — sense 1
If anyone has a conflict, say so now. — sense 1
Anyone is welcome to sit in on the rehearsal. — sense 2
She is faster over ten kilometers than anyone else on the team. — the comparative frame; else because she is on the team herself
Anyone who wants a copy should send me their address. — singular verb, singular they
It is anyone's guess how long the funding lasts.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on an-; the -one is unstressed and centers to [ˈɛniwən]. A stressed second element signals the two-word phrase any ONE (of them), which is a different structure. Free-choice anyone takes extra force on the first syllable
entries.русский: кто-нибудь (в вопросе и отрицании); любой (в утверждении) — книжнее, чем anybody
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; genitive anyone's
entries.register: neutral; the usual choice in edited prose
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun (nonassertive and free choice)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no plural, no gender.
entries.refers to: a person, human referents only. For things use anything, for places anywhere.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — Is anyone using this chair?, Anyone who wants a copy should email me. Back-reference is singular they: Anyone who wants a copy should send me their address.
entries.pattern: [negated verb] anyone · [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] anyone (question) · if / unless … anyone · hardly / scarcely / rarely / without … anyone · [comparative] than anyone · anyone [singular verb] (free choice) · anyone who / that [clause] · anyone's [noun] · anyone else
entries.contrast: Anyone against any one is the sharpest spelling trap in this family. One word is a pronoun meaning a person; two words is the determiner any plus the pronoun one, it means a single member of a stated set, it can refer to things as well as people, and it takes of: any one of the three routes will work. The test is of — if an of-phrase follows, it is two words. Against anybody, free choice of style. Against someone, the polarity rule, plus the ordering rule that keeps any- words out of subject position in front of a negated verb: ✗ Anyone didn't come → ✓ No one came.
entries.see also: anybody, anything, anyone else, someone, no one, everyone, someone else

entries.meaning: Refers to a thing without asserting that one exists. Two uses, plus a set of idioms built on it.
examples: I didn't hear anything unusual that night. — sense 1
Is there anything cheap on the menu? — sense 1, with the adjective following
If anything goes wrong, call the service line. — sense 1
That dog will eat anything. — sense 2, free choice
The second draft was anything but an improvement. — the idiom: it was worse
It doesn't taste anything like coffee.
If anything, the traffic was lighter than usual.

senses.head: Nonassertive
body: Under negation, in questions, and in conditionals: I didn't hear anything.

senses.head: Free choice
body: In affirmative clauses, meaning no matter what: She'll eat anything.

The idioms: anything but (= far from), anything like (= at all resembling, almost always under a negative), if anything (= if there is any difference at all), and the clause-final tag or anything (He didn't apologize or anything).
examples: I didn't hear anything unusual that night. — sense 1
Is there anything cheap on the menu? — sense 1, with the adjective following
If anything goes wrong, call the service line. — sense 1
That dog will eat anything. — sense 2, free choice
The second draft was anything but an improvement. — the idiom: it was worse
It doesn't taste anything like coffee.
If anything, the traffic was lighter than usual.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on an-; the final /ŋ/ is not /ŋɡ/, and casual speech gives [ˈɛniθɪn]. Free-choice anything takes a heavier first syllable and often a lengthened one: I'd eat AAAnything right now
entries.русский: что-нибудь (в вопросе и отрицании); что угодно (в утверждении)
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun (nonassertive and free choice)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant.
entries.refers to: things, ideas, events, and actions — non-human referents. Back-reference is it.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — Is anything wrong?, If anything goes wrong, call me, Nothing here is worth anything.
entries.pattern: [negated verb] anything · [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] anything (question) · if / unless … anything · anything [adjective] — the adjective follows (anything cheap) · anything to [verb] · anything that [clause] · anything but [adjective/noun] · anything like [noun] · anything [singular verb] (free choice)
entries.contrast: Polarity as with the rest of the any- words, plus two fixed phrases that reverse the meaning and are worth learning whole. Anything but means emphatically not: the exam was anything but easy says it was hard. Nothing but means only: nothing but trouble. Getting those two backwards inverts the sentence. Against something, the polarity rule and the scope wrinkle — I didn't buy anything denies the whole set, while I didn't buy something only works when something escapes the negation. Against everything, free-choice anything ranges over the set one member at a time (eat anything you like — pick one), while everything takes the set whole (eat everything — all of it).
entries.see also: anybody, anyone, something, nothing, everything, anything else

entries.meaning: Takes in every member of a group of people, without exception, and treats them as a single grammatical unit. The mismatch between its singular grammar and its plural meaning is the source of nearly every error in this file: the verb follows the grammar and stays singular, while the pronoun and the tag question follow the meaning and go plural.
examples: Everybody is already seated.
Everybody was handed a numbered ticket at the door.
The email went out to everybody on the distribution list.
Everybody brought their own folding chair. — singular verb, plural-form pronoun, both standard
Everybody's schedule shifted an hour when the flight changed.
Everybody's coming, aren't they? — plural tag on a singular verb
Everybody helped themselves to the leftovers.
entries.pronunciation note: every is two syllables in General American, /ˈɛvri/ — the medial vowel is normally dropped, and a careful three-syllable [ˈɛvəri] sounds like elocution. The /d/ taps between vowels, so the ordinary form is [ˈɛvribəɾi]. Stress never leaves the first syllable
entries.русский: все — но по-английски глагол в ед. ч.; разговорнее, чем everyone
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; genitive everybody's
entries.register: neutral; commoner than everyone in speech, less common in edited prose
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun (universal)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular though the meaning is plural; invariant, no gender.
entries.refers to: every person in the relevant group — human referents only. The group is whatever the context supplies: everyone in the room, in the company, in the world. For things use everything.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — Everybody is here, Everybody was given a badge, Everybody knows the story. ✗ Everybody are here. The pronoun that refers back is plural in form: Everybody brought their own lunch — standard American English, in edited prose as well as speech. So is the plural tag question on a singular verb: Everybody's coming, aren't they? The reflexive is themselves: Everybody helped themselves to the coffee.
entries.pattern: everybody [singular verb] · [verb] everybody · [preposition] everybody · everybody's [noun] · everybody [adjective/prepositional phrase] (everybody present, everybody in the room) · everybody else / everybody else's · everybody who / that [clause]
entries.contrast: Everybody and everyone are interchangeable, -one being the safer bet in formal writing. The important contrast is with all: everybody is invariably singular and takes a singular verb (Everybody is welcome), while all takes its number from whatever it refers to — plural for a set of people or countable things (All are welcome, All of the seats were taken), singular for a mass or an abstract totality (All is well, All of the paint was dry). The second contrast is the notorious one-word/two-word split, which everybody is mercifully spared — there is no ✗ every body in this sense, though every body does exist literally in a coroner's report. Its sibling everyone is not so lucky; see the note there.
entries.see also: everyone, everything, everybody else, everyone else, nobody, anybody, every

entries.meaning: Sweeps in every person in the group under discussion. It is the universal member of the -one set and stands opposite no one, which sweeps none of them in. Its grammar is singular and its meaning is plural, and English resolves the conflict by keeping the verb singular and letting everything downstream go plural.
examples: Everyone is accounted for.
Everyone in the two seminars needs a photo badge. — the plural noun in between does not make the verb plural
She thanked everyone who had stayed late.
Everyone should bring their own copy of the agenda. — singular verb, singular they
It was everyone's first time on a boat.
Every one of the applicants was interviewed twice. — two words, because of follows
Everyone here has read the report, haven't they?
entries.pronunciation note: /ˈɛvri/ with the medial vowel dropped, plus an unstressed -one that centers to [-wən]. Stress stays on ev-. If you hear a stress on the last syllable — every ONE — the speaker means the two-word phrase, and the grammar is different
entries.русский: все — по смыслу мн. ч., но глагол в ед. ч.; обычный вариант в редактируемой прозе
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; genitive everyone's
entries.register: neutral; the standard choice in edited American prose
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun (universal)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular with plural meaning; invariant, no gender.
entries.refers to: every person in the relevant group — human referents only. It cannot refer to things: for those use everything.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — Everyone is accounted for, Everyone has signed in, Everyone in the seminars needs a badge (the plural noun in between changes nothing). ✗ Everyone are. Back-reference is singular they/them/their, which the Chicago Manual of Style, the MLA Handbook, the APA Publication Manual, and the AP Stylebook all now accept — AP being the most cautious, still asking writers to reword where a rewrite is easy: Everyone should bring their own copy. Singular they still takes plural verb forms — they were, never ✗ they was.
entries.pattern: everyone [singular verb] · [verb] everyone · [preposition] everyone · everyone's [noun] · everyone [adjective/prepositional phrase] (everyone present, everyone here) · everyone else / everyone else's · everyone who / that [clause]
entries.contrast: One word or two — everyone against every one — is the single most tested spelling point in this family. One word is a pronoun meaning all the people: everyone laughed. Two words is the determiner every plus the pronoun one, it means each individual member of a stated set, it can refer to things, and it ✗ takes of: every one of the windows was cracked, I read every one of them. The test is mechanical — ✗ if an of-phrase follows, use two words; ✗ everyone of the windows is an error, and so is ✗ every one laughed for everyone laughed. Against all, the verb splits them: Everyone is welcome (singular) beside All are welcome (plural). Against everybody, free choice of register. One live dispute: Everyone knows each other is normal in speech and increasingly in print, but a strict reading objects that a singular subject cannot be reciprocal; They all know each other dodges it.
entries.see also: everybody, everything, everyone else, no one, anyone, someone, every one of

entries.meaning: Takes in the whole of the relevant set of things, with nothing left out. Its negative counterpart is nothing and its people counterparts are everyone and everybody. Like the rest of the compounds it is postmodified rather than premodified — everything valuable, never ✗ valuable everything.
examples: Everything is ready for the walkthrough.
They packed everything into a single trailer.
Everything valuable had already been moved to the safe.
Everything that could go wrong that morning did.
She lost everything but the photographs.
Everything in those crates needs a label before Friday.
Is that everything, or is there another box in the hall?
entries.pronunciation note: /ˈɛvri/ with the medial vowel dropped, stress on the first syllable; the final /ŋ/ is not /ŋɡ/, and casual speech gives [ˈɛvriθɪn]. In fast speech the /θ/ can weaken almost to nothing, leaving [ˈɛvriɪŋ]
entries.русский: всё — о вещах, фактах и обстоятельствах; глагол в ед. ч.
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun (universal)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular with plural or mass meaning; invariant.
entries.refers to: all the things, facts, or circumstances in view — non-human referents, count or mass. Back-reference is it: Everything is packed; it all fits. It reaches people only in loose idiom (she's everything to him), where the meaning is all that matters.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — Everything is ready, Everything has been moved, Everything in those boxes needs labeling. ✗ Everything are ready. Note that everything pairs with the singular all pattern rather than the plural one: Everything is fine beside All is well but All the lights are on.
entries.pattern: everything [singular verb] · [verb] everything · [preposition] everything · everything [adjective] — the adjective follows (everything valuable) · everything that [clause] · everything [reduced relative] · everything else · everything but [noun]
entries.contrast: Against all: all is a determiner when a noun follows (all the boxes) and takes the number of that noun, while everything stands alone and is always singular. Bare pronoun all meaning everything survives mainly in fixed and elevated phrasing (All is well, That's all), and in ordinary American prose everything is the natural choice. Against anything: everything takes the set whole (eat everything on the plate), free-choice anything takes any one member of it (eat anything on the plate). In relative clauses after everything, that is the overwhelming choice — everything that matters — but be clear about what kind of rule that is: restrictive which is perfectly grammatical (everything which matters appears in British and in American legal prose), and changing it to that is an American editing convention, not a repair. What is genuinely barred is what as a relative: ✗ everything what I own is nonstandard, and that is impossible in a nonrestrictive clause. And everything but the roof held means the roof failed; but here excludes.
entries.see also: everybody, everyone, everything else, nothing, anything, something

entries.meaning: Denies that any person satisfies the description. It is the written-out counterpart of nobody and the negative mirror of everyone, and like all the no- compounds it carries its own negative, so the verb after it is positive.
examples: No one is answering the service line today.
No one has signed the acknowledgment form yet.
She told no one where she was going.
No one admitted they had seen the memo. — singular verb, singular they
It is no one's job to check the backups, which is the problem.
No one in either department was notified.
No one else knew the combination.
entries.pronunciation note: written as two words but spoken as one unit, with primary stress on no and secondary stress on one; the linking /w/ ties them together, [ˈnoʊwʌn]. Unlike the -one of someone and anyone, this one keeps a fairly full vowel, because the phrase is not written solid
entries.русский: никто — только о людях; глагол в ед. ч. и без второго отрицания, в отличие от русского
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; genitive no one's
entries.register: neutral; the usual choice in edited American prose
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun (negative)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no gender.
entries.refers to: no person at all — human referents only. For things use nothing.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always, and the verb stays positive — No one is answering, No one has signed the form, No one in those departments was notified. Back-reference is singular they: No one admitted they had seen the memo.
entries.pattern: no one [positive singular verb] · [verb] no one · [preposition] no one · no one's [noun] · no one [adjective/prepositional phrase] (no one new, no one in the building) · no one else / no one else's · no one who / that [clause]
entries.contrast: Spelling first: in American English this is two words. No-one with a hyphen is a British variant that American editors open out to two words, and noone solid is always an error — it would be read as rhyming with moon, which is exactly why English never welded this compound the way it welded someone and anyone. Against nobody, identical meaning; no one is somewhat commoner in print. Against not … anyone, the same meaning with different emphasis and a different available position (I told no one / I didn't tell anyone, but only No one told me at the front of a clause). Do not confuse no one with none: none can be plural and can refer to things. And keep it separate from the two-word quantifier phrase in no one answer will satisfy everybody, where no is a determiner modifying the noun answer and one is a numeral.
entries.see also: nobody, nothing, none, no one else, everyone, anyone, nothing else, not a soul

entries.meaning: Denies that any person at all satisfies the description. It is the negative member of the -body set, the mirror image of everybody, and unlike anybody it carries its own negation and therefore works perfectly well as the subject of an ordinary positive verb.
examples: Nobody is home on Thursdays.
Nobody was hurt in the collision.
I called twice and reached nobody.
Nobody wanted to give their name to the reporter.
It was nobody's fault, and the report said so.
Nobody from the county has returned my calls.
Nobody important is going to read this memo — the adjective follows the pronoun.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on no-, whose vowel stays the full diphthong /oʊ/; the second element reduces and its /d/ taps, giving the everyday [ˈnoʊbəɾi] or [ˈnoʊbʌdi]. The word does not reduce further — a negative carries too much information to lose its first syllable
entries.русский: никто — то же, что no one, но чуть разговорнее; второго отрицания при глаголе не бывает
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; genitive nobody's
entries.register: neutral; slightly more conversational than no one
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun (negative)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no gender. The homograph in he's a nobody is a countable noun and pluralizes (a room full of nobodies).
entries.refers to: no person at all — human referents only, denying the whole class. For things use nothing; for a mixed or non-human set use none.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always, and the verb stays positive — Nobody is home, Nobody was hurt, Nobody knows. The negation lives in the pronoun, so the verb must not be negated as well: ✗ Nobody didn't come (unless you truly mean everybody came). Back-reference is singular they: Nobody wanted to give their name.
entries.pattern: nobody [positive singular verb] · [verb] nobody (I saw nobody) · [preposition] nobody · nobody's [noun] · nobody [adjective/prepositional phrase] (nobody important, nobody from the office) · nobody else / nobody else's · nobody who / that [clause]
entries.contrast: Against not … anybody, which means the same thing: I didn't tell anybody and I told nobody are both standard, the nobody version being more emphatic and more formal. Only nobody can stand in front of the verb — ✗ Anybody didn't call is not English; Nobody called is. The hard rule is that standard American English allows one negative per clause: ✗ I didn't see nobody is negative concord, systematic and rule-governed in African American English and in Southern and Appalachian vernacular but marked as nonstandard in edited prose; see nothing (negative concord). Against no one, pure style — identical meaning, no one commoner in writing. Against none, coverage: nobody is people-only and always singular, none covers people and things and can take a plural verb.
entries.see also: no one, nobody else, no one else, nothing, none, anybody, everybody, nothing (negative concord), no, not a soul

entries.meaning: Denies every member of a set already in view. It is the only member of this family whose number is genuinely open, which is why it needs a rule of its own rather than the flat always singular that governs the twelve compounds.
examples: None of the smoke detectors were working. — sense 1, plural, the ordinary modern choice
None of the water was safe to drink. — sense 2, mass noun, singular obligatory
None of the four finalists has ever held office. — sense 3, singular for the not one reading
We looked for a spare charger and found none. — bare, with the set understood
None were injured, according to the fire marshal.
He left an hour later, none the wiser. — sense 4, adverbial
She was none too pleased about the schedule change. — sense 4, adverbial

senses.head: Not any of a countable set
body: None of the smoke detectors were working. Plural verb, and the default in modern American usage.

senses.head: Not any of a mass
body: None of the water was safe to drink. Singular verb, obligatory.

senses.head: Emphatic not one
body: None of the four candidates has held elected office. Singular verb, chosen deliberately for the one-by-one reading.

senses.head: Adverbial, in fixed phrases
body: None the wiser, none too pleased — a different word class, modifying a comparative or an adjective.
examples: None of the smoke detectors were working. — sense 1, plural, the ordinary modern choice
None of the water was safe to drink. — sense 2, mass noun, singular obligatory
None of the four finalists has ever held office. — sense 3, singular for the not one reading
We looked for a spare charger and found none. — bare, with the set understood
None were injured, according to the fire marshal.
He left an hour later, none the wiser. — sense 4, adverbial
She was none too pleased about the schedule change. — sense 4, adverbial

entries.pronunciation note: rhymes with fun, not with bone — it is a perfect homophone of nun. The spelling misleads because the word is a worn-down compound of Old English ne + ān, not one, and the vowel followed one rather than the spelling. There is no weak form; a one-syllable negative does not reduce
entries.русский: ни один, никто; ничто — из уже названного множества; глагол в ед. или мн. ч.
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; no genitive (✗ none's)
entries.register: neutral; the emphatic singular is faintly formal
entries.type: indefinite pronoun (negative); historically the compound ne + one
entries.person / number: third person; number is variable, singular or plural depending on what it refers to — the whole point of the entry.
entries.refers to: people or things, unlike the rest of the no- words, which are split between the two. It can range over a count set (none of the applicants) or a mass (none of the milk). Used alone, it needs a set already established in the context: I looked for chairs and found none.
entries.agreement: The most misreported agreement fact in English. With a mass noun the verb is singular — None of the milk was spoiled, None of the evidence is admissible. With a plural count set the verb may be either, and the plural is older, commoner, and usually the better choice — None of the applicants were qualified. Plural agreement runs unbroken from Old English through Shakespeare to the present, and Merriam-Webster, the American Heritage Dictionary, Fowler, and Garner all endorse it; the claim that none must be singular because it means not one was invented by eighteenth-century commentators and has no basis in the history of the word. Choose the singular when you want to press the not one reading (None of the three has ever missed a deadline) or when the of-phrase is a mass noun. Be aware that the AP Stylebook is the conservative holdout, defaulting to the singular, so a newsroom copy desk may change your plural.
entries.pattern: none of [the/my/these + plural noun] + [plural or singular verb] · none of [the + mass noun] + [singular verb] · none of [them/us/you] · none [verb] (bare, with the set understood: None were injured) · [verb] none (I wanted coffee and there was none) · none the [comparative] (adverb: none the wiser) · none too [adjective] (adverb: none too pleased)
entries.contrast: Against no one and nobody: those are people only and always singular; none covers people and things and can go plural. Against neither: neither is for a set of exactly two and takes a singular verb in edited prose (Neither of the two plans works; neither of them are is common in speech and still changed by editors), while none is for three or more and may go either way (None of the five plans work). Against the determiner: none is not one. In modern English it never stands in front of a noun — ✗ none applicants — because that slot belongs to no (no applicants); the determiner-flavored partitive none of is treated at none of, and everything catalogued in this entry is the pronoun. Two adverbial idioms are a separate word class and never take a verb of their own: none the wiser, none the worse for it, none too happy.
entries.see also: no one, nobody, nothing, none of, neither, no, not a soul

entries.meaning: Denies that even one person satisfies the description, and denies it harder than nobody can. The phrase names the smallest possible number and then takes it away, which is the same move the minimizers make with quantities, and it is why not a soul so often ends a sentence about an empty place.
examples: Not a soul was waiting on the platform at that hour.
We knocked for ten minutes and not a soul came to the door.
Not a soul has called about the ad all week.
There wasn't a soul in the lot but the security guard. — the there-frame, where the negation sits on the verb and the phrase splits
Not a living soul outside the family knew about the loan. — the intensified form
He drove ninety miles down that road and saw not a soul. — the object slot, which is literary; ordinary speech says saw nobody
Not a soul would admit they had touched the thermostat. — singular verb, singular they
entries.pronunciation note: main stress on soul, whose vowel is the full diphthong /oʊ/ and never reduces. The weak form is on the article: a is /ə/ and never /eɪ/, and the /t/ of not taps between the two vowels, so the everyday form is [ˌnɑɾ ə ˈsoʊl]. Unmerged speakers keep /ɑ/ in not; the phrase carries one sweeping contour with the peak on soul
entries.русский: ни души — эмфатическое «совсем никого», с литературным оттенком
entries.case: none — invariant, one form for subject and object; no genitive is formed on it (rewrite as nobody's)
entries.register: neutral, with a literary edge. An American meets it in narrative, in complaint, and in weather-and-emptiness description, and it is perfectly printable in edited prose
entries.type: emphatic negative indefinite phrase, filling a pronoun slot
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular — and the singular is the whole point, since the phrase counts down to one person and then denies that one.
entries.refers to: no person at all — human referents only, and normally people who might have been present, seen, or heard from. Soul is a synecdoche for a person here and has no religious sense left in it. For things use nothing; for a set already in view, none.
entries.agreement: singular verb, and the verb stays positive — Not a soul was there, Not a soul has called all week. The negation lives inside the phrase, so a second one makes a double negative: ✗ Not a soul didn't come. Back-reference is singular they: Not a soul admitted they had seen it.
entries.pattern: not a soul [positive singular verb] · there wasn't a soul [prepositional phrase] · not a soul in [place] · not a soul for miles · not a living soul (the intensified form) · [verb] not a soul (literary; ordinary American English puts nobody in the object slot)
entries.contrast: Against nobody and no one, which state the same fact plainly: what not a soul adds is emphasis — not even one — which is why it is at home in front of the verb and in a short flat sentence (Not a soul came). It belongs to a family of emphatic negatives built on not a plus a minimal noun — not a one, not a thing, not a word, not a drop, and the dialectal nary a one — and it keeps their company in the negative-polarity frames not a soul in sight and not a soul for miles. Against none, which needs a set already established and can take a plural verb, where this phrase needs no set and is always singular. The intensifier not a living soul adds volume and nothing else. And keep the pronoun apart from the ordinary noun soul, which is alive and well in a kind soul, the poor soul, and the soul of the record — only inside this negative frame does the word mean simply person.
entries.variants: not a living soul, never a soul (literary), not a soul in sight, not one soul, nary a soul (Southern and Appalachian, and dialectal), not a one (of a set already named)
entries.see also: nobody, no one, none, nothing, not a one, not one, nary a one

entries.meaning: Denies the existence of any relevant thing. It has four uses in ordinary American English.
examples: Nothing is working in this building today. — sense 1
There's nothing new in the second report. — sense 1, adjective following
They lost the opener four to nothing. — sense 2
The apology meant nothing to the people who were laid off. — sense 3
That contract has brought us nothing but headaches. — sense 4, nothing but = only
We drove four hours for nothing.
Nothing that came out of that meeting surprised me.

senses.head: Not a thing
body: The core sense: Nothing arrived in the mail.

senses.head: Zero, in scores and arithmetic
body: We lost three to nothing. Informal, alongside zip, zilch, and the tennis love.

senses.head: Something or someone of no value or importance
body: The award means nothing to her. He's nothing without that team.

senses.head: Fixed phrases
body: Nothing but (= only), nothing like (= not at all resembling), nothing if not (= emphatically), for nothing (= free, or in vain), nothing doing (= a refusal), think nothing of it.
examples: Nothing is working in this building today. — sense 1
There's nothing new in the second report. — sense 1, adjective following
They lost the opener four to nothing. — sense 2
The apology meant nothing to the people who were laid off. — sense 3
That contract has brought us nothing but headaches. — sense 4, nothing but = only
We drove four hours for nothing.
Nothing that came out of that meeting surprised me.

entries.pronunciation note: the vowel is /ʌ/, not /oʊ/ — nothing does not rhyme with no thing, and mispronouncing it [ˈnoʊθɪŋ] is the commonest learner error on this word. Casual American English gives [ˈnʌθɪn] and, faster still, [ˈnʌʔn̩] — the nuthin' of ordinary speech. Stress on the first syllable
entries.русский: ничто, ничего — о вещах; глагол остаётся утвердительным, второго отрицания нет
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; nothing's in running text is almost always nothing is or nothing has, not a genitive
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun (negative)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant.
entries.refers to: no thing at all — non-human referents: objects, ideas, events, amounts. Applied to a person it is an insult of the he's nothing to me kind, where the sense is of no importance. Back-reference is it.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always, and the verb stays positive — Nothing is working, Nothing has changed, Nothing in these files matches the invoice. ✗ Nothing doesn't work is a double negative unless you mean everything works.
entries.pattern: nothing [positive singular verb] · [verb] nothing · [preposition] nothing · nothing [adjective] — the adjective follows (nothing new) · nothing to [verb] · nothing that [clause] · nothing but [noun] · nothing like [noun] · for nothing · nothing else
entries.contrast: Nothing but means only — nothing but trouble is all trouble. Anything but means far from — anything but trouble is no trouble at all. They look parallel and mean opposite things, and swapping them inverts the sentence. Against not … anything, same meaning with different weight: I said nothing is heavier than I didn't say anything, and only nothing works as a subject (Nothing was said). The one-negative rule applies: ✗ I didn't say nothing is negative concord, nonstandard in edited American English; see nothing (negative concord). Two double negatives that are perfectly standard, though: litotes, where the second negative is deliberate and the meaning turns positive (That's not nothing, the response was not uncommon), and negation across a clause boundary (I didn't say nothing was wrong — two clauses, two independent negatives, entirely grammatical).
entries.see also: nobody, no one, none, everything, anything, something, nothing else, nothing (negative concord), zilch, nada, bupkis, zip, diddly, diddly-squat, squat, not a soul

entries.term: all else, much else, little else
entries.meaning: Three quantifiers wearing the same else the compounds wear, and meaning the remainder of the set. They are worth an entry of their own because the quantifier in front of else keeps its polarity: much else leans on a negative, little else is already negative, and all else has retired into a handful of set phrases.
examples: All else being equal, take the earlier flight. — the fixed phrase, which is where all else mostly lives
When all else fails, call the manufacturer and ask for the service department.
Get the foundation right and all else follows.
There wasn't much else to do but wait for the tide. — nonassertive, licensed by the negative in front of it
I don't remember much else about that summer.
Little else in the report is worth the time it takes to read it. — positive verb; the negation sits inside little
The fire took the barn, and little else on the property was touched.
entries.pronunciation note: main stress lands on else in all three, exactly as it does after the twelve compounds; the /l/ of all runs straight into the vowel of else with no break, [ˌɔl ˈɛls], and the /t/ of little is a tap or a glottal stop before its syllabic /l/, [ˈlɪɾl̩ ˈɛls]. Americans who merge cot and caught have /ɑl/ in all. No weak forms — else takes the stress and the quantifier in front of it keeps its full vowel
entries.русский: всё остальное; многое другое; мало что ещё — об оставшемся, только о вещах
entries.case: none — invariant, one form for subject and object, and no genitive (✗ all else's, ✗ little else's)
entries.register: neutral. Much else and little else are ordinary written and spoken English; all else is faintly formal and lives almost entirely inside three fixed phrases
entries.type: quantifying indefinite pronouns postmodified by else
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no plural and no gender.
entries.refers to: the remainder of a set of things, facts, or considerations — whatever is left over once the thing just named is set aside. Non-human referents: for people the language uses everybody else and nobody else, and there is no ✗ much else about persons. Back-reference is it.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — All else is detail, Little else matters, Not much else was said that evening. Little else carries its own negation, so the verb after it stays positive: ✓ Little else survived the fire, ✗ Little else didn't survive.
entries.pattern: all else being equal · when all else fails · all else [singular verb] (all else follows) · [negated verb] much else (I don't remember much else) · not much else to [verb] · little else [positive singular verb] · little else but / than [noun] · there is little else [infinitive]
entries.contrast: Else subtracts here exactly as it does after the compounds, but the words in front of it are quantifiers, so each one keeps its own quantifier behavior — and polarity is the practical difference. Much else is nonassertive: in ordinary usage it wants a negative, a question, or a conditional in front of it (✓ I don't remember much else, ✓ Was there much else?, and ✗ I remember much else is not idiomatic), which is the same restriction bare much lives under; the affirmative there is much else to admire does survive in formal writing, just as much has been written does. Little else supplies the negation itself and takes a positive verb — Little else was salvageable — and it is not the same as a little else, which is not English at all. All else is the universal member and is nearly frozen: all else being equal, when all else fails, all else follows, and elsewhere an American writes everything else instead — everything else was fine is ordinary, all else was fine reads like a translation. Keep the determiners out of it: all and little in front of a noun (all the rest, little hope) belong to the determiner dictionary, at all and little.
entries.variants: nothing else and everything else (the compound equivalents, and the commoner words for the same facts), not much else, precious little else, all the rest
entries.see also: everything else, nothing else, something else, anything else, all, much, little

entries.meaning: Refers to a further or different person without asserting that one exists. It carries both of bare anybody's lives — nonassertive under a negative, a question, or a condition, and free choice in affirmatives — and adds the subtraction that else contributes: whoever is already in view is taken out of the set.
examples: Did anybody else hear that? — nonassertive, in a question
I didn't tell anybody else about the transfer. — nonassertive, under a negative
If anybody else wants a ride, tell them to wait out front. — conditional, with singular they
Anybody else would have walked out an hour ago. — free choice
He finished ahead of anybody else in his age group. — the comparative, where else is doing real work
Hardly anybody else stayed for the second session.
It is anybody else's guess where the money went. — the genitive, with the -s on else
entries.pronunciation note: main stress moves onto else, which is what welds the phrase into one unit; anybody keeps a secondary stress on an-, its /d/ taps between vowels, and its final vowel runs straight into else with no break, giving the everyday [ˌɛnibəɾi ˈɛls]. The genitive anybody else's adds a syllable, [ˌɛnibəɾi ˈɛlsəz]
entries.русский: кто-нибудь ещё, кто-то другой — кроме уже названного; разговорнее, чем anyone else
entries.case: none for the base form — one invariant shape for subject and object; genitive anybody else's
entries.register: neutral; a shade more conversational than anyone else
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun postmodified by else (nonassertive and free choice)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no plural, no gender.
entries.refers to: any additional or different person — human referents only, with someone already named and now excluded, and with no commitment that such a further person exists. For a thing use anything else.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — Is anybody else coming?, If anybody else objects, say so now, Hardly anybody else was there. Back-reference is singular they, which is standard American English in edited prose as well as speech: If anybody else wants a ride, tell them to wait out front.
entries.pattern: [negated verb] anybody else (I didn't ask anybody else) · [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] anybody else (question) · if / unless … anybody else · hardly / scarcely / rarely / without … anybody else · [comparative] than anybody else · anybody else [singular verb] (free choice) · anybody else who / that [clause] · anybody else's [noun] · anybody else [adjective] (anybody else new)
entries.contrast: Identical in meaning to anyone else and one notch more conversational, exactly as anybody is to anyone; edited prose leans to the -one form. Polarity runs as it does for bare anybody: anybody else under a negative, in a question, or in a conditional, and somebody else in a plain statement or in the question that is really an offer (Would somebody else like to try?). The ordering rule holds too — an any- compound cannot sit in front of the negative that licenses it, so only nobody else can head a clause: ✓ Nobody else knew, ✗ Anybody else didn't know. In the comparative frame the else is doing real logical work: she is faster than anybody else on the team keeps her out of the very set she is being measured against, where the else-less version quietly puts her in it. The possessive puts the -s on else: ✓ anybody else's guess, ✗ anybody's else guess; see someone else's.
entries.see also: anybody, anyone else, anything else, somebody else, nobody else, everybody else, someone else's

entries.meaning: Refers to a further or different person without asserting that one exists. It carries both of bare anyone's lives — nonassertive under a negative, a question, or a condition, and free choice in affirmatives — and adds the subtraction that else contributes: whoever is already in view is taken out of the set.

I didn't tell anyone else about the transfer. — nonassertive, under a negative
If anyone else wants a ride, tell them to meet us out front. — conditional, with singular they
Anyone else would have walked out an hour ago. — free choice
She finished ahead of anyone else in her age group. — the comparative, where else is doing real work
Hardly anyone else showed up for the second session.
It is anyone else's guess where the money went. — the genitive, with the -s on else

The /n/ links straight into the vowel of else with no break, [ˌɛniwən ˈɛls]. The genitive anyone else's adds a syllable, [ˌɛniwən ˈɛlsəz]
entries.русский: кто-нибудь ещё, кто-то другой — кроме уже названного лица
entries.case: none for the base form; genitive anyone else's
entries.register: neutral; anybody else is the more conversational twin
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun postmodified by else (nonassertive and free choice)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no plural, no gender.
entries.refers to: any additional or different person — human referents only, with someone already named and now excluded, and with no commitment that such a further person exists. For a thing use anything else.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — Is anyone else coming?, If anyone else objects, say so now, Hardly anyone else was there. Back-reference is singular they: If anyone else wants a ride, tell them to meet us out front.
entries.pattern: [negated verb] anyone else (I didn't ask anyone else) · [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] anyone else (question) · if / unless … anyone else · hardly / scarcely / rarely / without … anyone else · [comparative] than anyone else · anyone else [singular verb] (free choice) · anyone else who / that [clause] · anyone else's [noun] · anyone else [adjective] (anyone else new)
entries.contrast: Polarity runs exactly as it does for bare anyone: anyone else under a negative, in a question, or in a conditional, and someone else in a plain statement or in the question that is really an offer (Would someone else like to try?). The comparative frame is where this phrase does its most useful work. In she is faster than anyone else on the team, the else is doing real logical work: without it the sentence puts her into the very set she is being measured against. The else-less version is common and almost never misunderstood, but careful writing keeps the else — more than anyone else, before anyone else, faster than anyone else. Against no one else, the pair not … anyone else and no one else mean the same thing, and only no one else can head a clause: ✓ No one else knew, ✗ Anyone else didn't know — the same ordering rule that governs bare anyone. The possessive puts the -s on else: ✓ anyone else's guess, ✗ anyone's else guess; see someone else's.
entries.see also: anyone, anybody, anybody else, anything else, someone else, no one else, everyone else, someone else's

entries.meaning: Asks after or denies any further thing beyond what has already been mentioned. Else here means other than the one already in view, and it follows the pronoun — this is the fixed order for the whole family.
examples: Is there anything else you need before I lock up?
I couldn't find anything else in the file cabinet.
If there's anything else on the invoice, flag it now.
Anything else would have been an improvement on that ending.
She never mentioned anything else about the phone call.
Do you want fries, a drink, anything else?
entries.pronunciation note: the main stress moves onto else, which is what welds the phrase into a single unit; anything keeps a secondary stress on its first syllable. The /ŋ/ links straight into the following vowel with no break between the words
entries.русский: что-нибудь ещё, что-то другое — кроме уже названного; «Anything else?» — «Ещё что-нибудь?»
entries.case: none — invariant; the genitive anything else's is theoretically possible and practically never used
entries.register: neutral; the counter-service question Anything else? is one of the most-heard sentences in American commercial life
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun postmodified by else (nonassertive and free choice)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant.
entries.refers to: any additional or different thing — non-human referents, in a context where some thing has already been named or supplied.
entries.agreement: singular verb — Is there anything else that needs signing?, Nothing else is open at this hour.
entries.pattern: [negated verb] anything else · Is / was there anything else …? (question) · if … anything else · anything else [adjective] (anything else useful) · anything else to [verb] · anything else that [clause]
entries.contrast: Polarity works exactly as it does for bare anything, which means the service-counter question splits two ways. Anything else? is neutral and open — it asks whether there is more. Something else? is an offer, and it presumes there is. A waiter who says Anything else for you? is closing out; one who says Can I get you something else? is selling. Under a negative, anything else is the only option: ✗ I don't want something else is odd unless something else escapes the negation. Against nothing else, the same relationship anything has with nothing: I don't need anything else equals I need nothing else, the second being heavier.
entries.see also: anything, anyone else, something else, nothing else, everything else, someone else

entries.meaning: Sweeps in all the members of a group other than the ones just mentioned. Its grammar is singular and its meaning is plural, exactly as with bare everybody, and English resolves the conflict the same way: the verb stays singular while the pronoun, the reflexive, and the tag question all go plural.
examples: Everybody else is already inside.
I stayed to close up; everybody else went home at six.
She got the memo a day after everybody else.
Everybody else's flights were canceled, and ours somehow left on time.
Everybody else got their refund within a week. — singular verb, singular they
Like everybody else in that office, he pretended not to have seen it.
Everybody else helped themselves to the leftovers. — singular verb, plural reflexive
entries.pronunciation note: main stress on else, secondary on ev-; every keeps its medial vowel dropped, as always in General American, and the /d/ of -body taps, so the ordinary form is [ˌɛvribəɾi ˈɛls]. The genitive everybody else's adds a syllable, [ˌɛvribəɾi ˈɛlsəz]
entries.русский: все остальные — все, кроме уже названных; глагол в ед. ч.

entries.register: neutral; commoner than everyone else in speech, less common in edited prose
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun postmodified by else (universal)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular though the meaning is plural; invariant, no gender.
entries.refers to: all the other people — every person in the group except the one or ones already named. Human referents only. For things use everything else.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — Everybody else is already inside, Everybody else has left for the day. ✗ Everybody else are. Everything downstream then goes plural: the pronoun is singular they (Everybody else got their refund), the reflexive is themselves (Everybody else helped themselves), and the tag question is plural (Everybody else is coming, aren't they?).

entries.contrast: Identical in meaning to everyone else and a shade more conversational, exactly as everybody is to everyone. Against bare everybody, else subtracts the people already in view: everybody laughed includes you, everybody else laughed does not. Against all the others and the others, which mean the same thing and take a plural verb — All the others were late beside Everybody else was late. The possessive is everybody else's, with the -s on else; ✗ everybody's else is the seventeenth-century pattern and now simply wrong.

She got the memo a day after everyone else.
Everyone else's flights were canceled, and ours somehow left on time.
Everyone else got their refund within a week. — singular verb, singular they

entries.meaning: Takes in the whole of the remaining set of things, with the named items subtracted. It is the workhorse phrase for closing a list — the deposit, the inspection, and everything else — and stays grammatically singular however long the list gets.
examples: Everything else is already in the truck.
We salvaged the photographs; everything else was ruined.
Everything else on the list can wait until Monday.
Compared with the roof, everything else was cheap.
Everything else that came out of that audit was routine.
Fix the leak first and worry about everything else later.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on else; the /ŋ/ of -thing links straight into the vowel of else, so there is no break between the two words
entries.русский: всё остальное — все прочие вещи, кроме уже названных
entries.case: none — invariant; no genitive in ordinary use
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun postmodified by else (universal)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular; invariant.
entries.refers to: all the other things — every item in view except the ones already named. Non-human referents. Back-reference is it.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — Everything else is in the truck, Everything else has been packed. ✗ Everything else are.
entries.pattern: everything else [singular verb] · [verb] everything else · [preposition] everything else · everything else [adjective] (everything else valuable) · everything else that [clause]
entries.contrast: Against bare everything, else subtracts what has already been mentioned. Against all the rest and the remainder, which mean the same but take their number from what they refer to (All the rest were shipped) where everything else is invariably singular (Everything else was shipped). Against nothing else, its negative mirror. And note that the everything words are the natural repair when a sentence would otherwise strand bare all: All was fine reads as scripture and Everything was fine reads as English, with Everything else was fine the form to reach for once the named items have been subtracted.

entries.meaning: Denies that any person other than the ones already named satisfies the description. It is the negative member of the -one + else set and the mirror of everyone else, and like all the no- compounds it carries its own negative, so the verb that follows it is positive.
examples: No one else is coming, so we can start.
No one else has a key to that cabinet.
She told no one else what the offer actually was.
No one else admitted they had seen the email. — singular verb, singular they
It was no one else's business, and she said so. — the genitive, with the -s on else
There was no one else in the building at that hour.
No one else in the department had the clearance.
entries.pronunciation note: main stress on else, secondary on no-; all three words run together as a single unit, [ˌnoʊwʌn ˈɛls], with the linking /w/ tying no to one and the /n/ tying one to else. The genitive no one else's adds a syllable, [ˌnoʊwʌn ˈɛlsəz]
entries.русский: никто другой, больше никто — кроме уже названных
entries.case: none for the base form; genitive no one else's
entries.register: neutral; the usual choice in edited American prose, with nobody else a shade more conversational
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun postmodified by else (negative)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no gender.
entries.refers to: no other person — human referents only, with one or more people already named and now excluded from the denial. For a thing use nothing else.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always, and the verb stays positive — No one else is coming, No one else has a key, No one else in those departments was notified. The negation lives in the pronoun, so the verb must not be negated as well: ✗ No one else doesn't have a key unless you truly mean the reverse. Back-reference is singular they: No one else admitted they had seen the email.
entries.pattern: no one else [positive singular verb] · [verb] no one else (I told no one else) · [preposition] no one else · no one else's [noun] · no one else [adjective/prepositional phrase] (no one else new, no one else in the building) · no one else who / that [clause] · no one else to [verb]
entries.contrast: Spelling first: two words in American English, exactly as bare no one is; ✗ noone else is an error and no-one else is the British hyphenation. Against not … anyone else, the same meaning with different weight and a different range of positions — I told no one else and I didn't tell anyone else are both standard, but only no one else can head a clause (✓ No one else knew, ✗ Anyone else didn't know). Against the -body twin nobody else, identical in meaning and a notch more conversational. Against everyone else, its exact mirror: one sweeps in all the others, the other sweeps in none of them. The one-negative rule holds here as everywhere in this file: ✗ There wasn't no one else there is negative concord, systematic in African American English and in Southern and Appalachian vernacular and nonstandard in edited prose; see nothing (negative concord). The possessive goes on else: ✓ no one else's business, ✗ no one's else business.
entries.see also: no one, nobody, nobody else, nothing else, everyone else, anyone else, none, someone else's

entries.meaning: Denies that any person other than the ones already named satisfies the description. It is the negative member of the -body + else set and the mirror of everybody else, and like all the no- compounds it carries its own negative, so the verb that follows it is positive.

entries.meaning: Denies every remaining thing once the named ones are set aside. Its most common life is emphatic: nothing else matters is a claim about priority, not about inventory.
examples: Nothing else matters if the foundation is bad.
The hail took the skylight and nothing else.
There was nothing else to do but wait for the tow truck.
Nothing else in the report contradicted her account.
He wanted the corner office and nothing else.
Nothing else was damaged in the flood, which was pure luck.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on else; nothing keeps its /ʌ/ and a secondary stress, and the /ŋ/ links straight into the following vowel. Casual speech gives [ˌnʌʔn̩ ˈɛls]
entries.русский: ничто другое, больше ничего — кроме уже названного

entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun postmodified by else (negative)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular; invariant.
entries.refers to: no other thing — non-human referents, with something already named and now excluded from the denial.
entries.agreement: singular verb, and the verb stays positive — Nothing else matters, Nothing else was damaged. ✗ Nothing else doesn't matter unless you mean the reverse.
entries.pattern: nothing else [positive singular verb] · [verb] nothing else · nothing else [adjective] (nothing else useful) · nothing else to [verb] · nothing else that [clause] · there was nothing else for it (fixed idiom)
entries.contrast: Against not … anything else, the same meaning with more weight and a wider range of positions: Nothing else was damaged has no anything equivalent at the front of a clause (✗ Anything else wasn't damaged). Against everything else, its exact mirror. The one-negative rule holds here as everywhere: ✗ There wasn't nothing else is negative concord, not standard edited English. The idiom there was nothing else for it — meaning there was no alternative — is chiefly British and reads as borrowed in American prose; the American equivalent is there was no other choice.

entries.meaning: Names a person other than the one under discussion. The subtraction is the whole content of else, which is why the phrase almost always needs a previously named person to work against.
examples: Somebody else is handling that account now.
If I can't make it, they'll send somebody else.
She's already told somebody else the whole story.
That was somebody else's idea, not mine. — the genitive, with the -s on else
Somebody else left their coat on the back of my chair. — singular verb, singular they
Ask somebody else who was actually in the room.
Could somebody else take the early shift? — a request, so some- survives inside a question
entries.pronunciation note: main stress lands on else and the phrase is spoken as one unit; somebody keeps a secondary stress on some-, its /d/ taps, and its final vowel links straight into else, giving the everyday [ˌsʌmbəɾi ˈɛls]. The genitive somebody else's adds a syllable, [ˌsʌmbəɾi ˈɛlsəz]
entries.русский: кто-то другой — не тот, о ком шла речь; разговорнее, чем someone else

entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun postmodified by else (assertive)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no plural, no gender.
entries.refers to: a different person — some person other than the one already named or implied. Human referents only. For a thing use something else.
entries.agreement: singular verb — Somebody else is handling that account now, Somebody else has already reported it. Back-reference is singular they: Somebody else left their coat.
entries.pattern: somebody else [singular verb] · [verb] somebody else · [preposition] somebody else · somebody else's [noun] · somebody else [adjective] (somebody else new) · somebody else who / that [clause] · somebody else to [verb]
entries.contrast: Identical in meaning to someone else and a shade more conversational, exactly as somebody is to someone. Against anybody else the difference is polarity: some- in plain affirmative statements, any- under a negative, in a question, or after if — with the standing exception that a question which is really an offer or request keeps some- (Could somebody else take the early shift?). Else always follows, never precedes: ✓ somebody else, ✗ else somebody, and it never attaches to an ordinary noun — ✗ the man else has to become the other man. That is the practical relationship between else and another: somebody else and another person say the same thing, one with a postmodifier and one with a determiner. The possessive goes on else: ✓ somebody else's coat, ✗ somebody's else coat; see someone else's.
entries.see also: somebody, someone else, something else, anybody else, nobody else, everybody else, somebody else's

examples: Someone else is handling that account now.
If I can't make it, they'll send someone else.
She's already told someone else the whole story.
That was someone else's idea, not mine.
Someone else left their coat on the back of my chair.
Ask someone else who was actually in the room.
