entries.meaning: Marks something as belonging to a person other than the one in view. Grammatically it behaves exactly like John's or the neighbor's: it fills the determiner slot, so it cannot combine with the, a, or this — ✓ someone else's problem, ✗ the someone else's problem — and it can equally stand alone as a full noun phrase with no noun after it, that coat is someone else's.
examples: That's someone else's problem now.
I picked up someone else's umbrella by mistake.
Someone else's keys are sitting on the break-room counter.
You can't sign someone else's name on a federal form.
It was nobody else's business, and she said so.
Everyone else's flight got canceled that night.
This jacket isn't mine — it must be someone else's. — standing alone as a full noun phrase, with no noun after it
entries.pronunciation note: the genitive -s attaches to else and is pronounced /əz/ after the /s/, adding a syllable: [ˌsʌmwʌn ˈɛlsəz]. Main stress stays on else
entries.русский: чужой, кого-то другого — притяжательная форма; по-русски чаще просто «чужой»
entries.case: possessive (genitive) — the one case-marked form in this whole family, which is why it is catalogued as a separate entry. It does the two jobs any genitive does: it fills the determiner slot in front of a noun, exactly as a name plus apostrophe-s does, and it stands alone as a full noun phrase with no noun after it. Both uses are shown in the examples below, and the determiner-slot use is cross-referenced to the determiner dictionary
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: genitive of a compound indefinite pronoun modified by else
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no gender.
entries.refers to: the possessions, attributes, or responsibilities of some person other than the one named. Human referents only.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the noun it modifies, not with the pronoun: Someone else's keys are on the counter (plural noun, plural verb), Someone else's car is in my spot (singular noun, singular verb).
entries.pattern: someone else's [noun] · anybody / anyone / everybody / everyone / nobody / no one else's [noun] · somebody else's [noun] (the -body variant) · [verb] someone else's [noun] · [subject] is someone else's (predicative, standing alone with no noun after it) · that's someone else's [noun]
entries.contrast: The apostrophe goes on else, not on the pronoun. ✓ someone else's coat; ✗ someone's else coat; ✗ someone's else's coat. The rejected form is not an invention — somebody's else was the normal seventeenth- and eighteenth-century pattern, and it lost to somebody else's by about 1850, which is why old books look wrong to modern eyes. The same rule governs anyone else's, everybody else's, and no one else's. The wh- parallel who else's is grammatical (Who else's signature is on this?) but strikes many ears as awkward, and most writers rewrite it. Things do not take this genitive comfortably: nothing else's and everything else's are avoided in favor of of (the cost of everything else). Compare the determiner treatment at somebody else's.
entries.see also: someone else, someone, everyone else, no one else, anyone else, somebody else's

entries.meaning: Names a thing other than the one in view. Two uses, and the second is idiomatic.
examples: Let's talk about something else. — sense 1
Something else is going on here that nobody's saying out loud. — sense 1
If the sea bass is gone, I'll order something else. — sense 1
That thunderstorm last night was something else. — sense 2
Her second album is something else entirely. — sense 2
He asked for something else to read on the flight.

senses.head: A different or additional thing
body: Let's talk about something else. This is the ordinary sense and takes the usual postmodifiers.

senses.head: Remarkable — good or bad
body: That storm was something else. Informal, predicative only, and applicable to people as well as things. The tone is admiring by default and can turn sardonic with the right delivery.
examples: Let's talk about something else. — sense 1
Something else is going on here that nobody's saying out loud. — sense 1
If the sea bass is gone, I'll order something else. — sense 1
That thunderstorm last night was something else. — sense 2
Her second album is something else entirely. — sense 2
He asked for something else to read on the flight.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on else, with the reductions of something still available in the first half: [ˌsʌmpm̩ ˈɛls]. In the remarkable sense the phrase is often drawn out with a fall on else — she's something ELSE
entries.русский: что-то другое, нечто иное; разг. «нечто особенное, нечто» (she's something else)
entries.case: none — invariant; no genitive in ordinary use
entries.register: neutral in sense 1; informal and admiring in sense 2
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun postmodified by else (assertive)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular; invariant.
entries.refers to: a different thing in sense 1 — non-human. In sense 2 it can be predicated of a person (that kid is something else), which is the one place in this family where a -thing compound reaches a human referent.
entries.agreement: singular verb — Something else is going on here, Something else has to give.

entries.meaning: Refers to a place without committing to which one, or to whether such a place exists. Two uses plus a quantity idiom.
examples: I can't find my other glove anywhere. — sense 1
Did you go anywhere interesting over the break? — sense 1, adjective following
Sit anywhere you like; the seats aren't assigned. — sense 2
That truck will get you anywhere with a road. — sense 2
We're expecting anywhere from twenty to fifty people. — sense 3
The bid wasn't anywhere near what the house was worth.

senses.head: Nonassertive
body: Under a negative, in a question, or in a conditional: I can't find it anywhere.

senses.head: Free choice
body: In affirmatives, meaning no matter where: Sit anywhere you like.

senses.head: Quantity range
body: Anywhere from twenty to fifty people — an approximator, and the one use where anywhere has nothing to do with place.
examples: I can't find my other glove anywhere. — sense 1
Did you go anywhere interesting over the break? — sense 1, adjective following
Sit anywhere you like; the seats aren't assigned. — sense 2
That truck will get you anywhere with a road. — sense 2
We're expecting anywhere from twenty to fifty people. — sense 3
The bid wasn't anywhere near what the house was worth.

entries.русский: где-нибудь, куда-нибудь; где угодно, куда угодно — наречие места, а не местоимение

entries.register: neutral

entries.refers to: a place, location, or destination, unspecified and with no commitment that one exists. In the quantity idiom anywhere from … to … it refers to a point on a numerical range instead.
entries.agreement: as an adverb it triggers no verb agreement of its own; the verb agrees with the clause's own subject — The keys are not anywhere in this house. Under a negative it must follow the negation: ✓ I didn't go anywhere, ✗ Anywhere I didn't go.
entries.pattern: [negated verb] anywhere (I can't find it anywhere) · [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] anywhere (question) · if … anywhere · anywhere [adjective] (anywhere quiet) · anywhere near [noun] · anywhere from [number] to [number] · [preposition] anywhere (from anywhere, to anywhere with a runway)
entries.contrast: These four -where words are adverbs, not pronouns — they fill an adverbial slot, not a noun-phrase slot, so I went somewhere patterns with I went home, not with I saw something. They are catalogued here because they take the same four stems, obey the same polarity rule, take the same postmodifiers (anywhere quiet, nowhere to go), and take else the same way (somewhere else). The honest wrinkle is that they do occasionally head a genuine noun phrase after a preposition — from nowhere, in somewhere warm — which is why grammars disagree about their category. Against somewhere, polarity. Anywhere near is a fixed intensifier under a negative: not anywhere near enough is far short.
entries.see also: somewhere, everywhere, nowhere, anything, someplace, anyplace, everyplace, noplace

entries.meaning: Covers the whole set of relevant places, with none left out. It is the universal member of the -where group and the mirror of nowhere.
examples: There was construction dust everywhere.
Everywhere I go, somebody asks about the merger.
The recall notice went everywhere except to the people who owned the car.
By ten o'clock everywhere downtown was closed. — the colloquial subject use, singular verb
She has looked everywhere else already.
Reports came in from everywhere between Denver and Omaha.
entries.pronunciation note: /ˈɛvri/ with the medial vowel dropped, as in everyone; -where keeps its full /ɛr/ and a secondary stress. Americans outside the Northeast pronounce the vowel of -where the same as in air and bear
entries.русский: везде, повсюду — наречие места
entries.case: none — adverbs take no case
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: compound indefinite adverb (universal) — not a pronoun
entries.person / number: invariant.
entries.refers to: all the places in view, or metaphorically all the parts of something (there's dust everywhere).
entries.agreement: no agreement of its own as an adverb. In the colloquial subject-like use it takes a singular verb — Everywhere was closed by nine — and in fronted emphatic position the clause inverts: Everywhere I looked there was another form to sign.
entries.pattern: [verb] everywhere · everywhere [clause] (everywhere I go) · everywhere [adjective/participle] (everywhere visible) · from / to everywhere · everywhere else
entries.contrast: Against all over and all around, which are its ordinary spoken equivalents (dust all over the place). Against anywhere, the same universal-versus-free-choice split that separates everything from anything: go everywhere covers the whole map, go anywhere picks one point at will. The construction everywhere I go is a free relative adverb — everywhere is doing the work of in every place where — and it needs no that: everywhere that I go is not wrong, merely redundant, and editors cut the that. The colloquial Everywhere was closed treats the adverb as a subject; it is idiomatic and widespread but still flagged by some editors, and Everything was closed or All the stores were closed avoids the argument.
entries.see also: somewhere, anywhere, nowhere, everything, everything else

entries.meaning: Denies every place. Its life outside literal location is unusually rich for a negative adverb.
examples: The service road led nowhere. — sense 1
This argument is getting us nowhere. — sense 2
A pickup came out of nowhere and took the mirror off. — sense 3
They bought forty acres in the middle of nowhere. — sense 3
It was nowhere near enough money to cover the repairs. — sense 3, degree
Nowhere is that clearer than in the last chapter. — fronted, with inversion
There was nowhere to sit and nowhere to put the bags.

senses.head: No place
body: The trail led nowhere.

senses.head: No progress
body: This conversation is getting us nowhere.

senses.head: Fixed phrases
body: Out of nowhere (suddenly and without warning), the middle of nowhere (remote), nowhere near (far from), nowhere to be found, nowhere to turn, and the attributive a nowhere job.
examples: The service road led nowhere. — sense 1
This argument is getting us nowhere. — sense 2
A pickup came out of nowhere and took the mirror off. — sense 3
They bought forty acres in the middle of nowhere. — sense 3
It was nowhere near enough money to cover the repairs. — sense 3, degree
Nowhere is that clearer than in the last chapter. — fronted, with inversion
There was nowhere to sit and nowhere to put the bags.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on no-, whose vowel stays the full /oʊ/; -where takes a clear secondary stress. Unlike nothing, this compound keeps the vowel the spelling promises
entries.русский: нигде, никуда — наречие; вынесенное вперёд требует инверсии, чего в русском нет
entries.case: none — adverbs take no case
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: compound indefinite adverb (negative) — not a pronoun, though it takes noun-phrase position after prepositions
entries.person / number: invariant.
entries.refers to: no place at all. After a preposition it behaves like a noun (out of nowhere, the middle of nowhere), which is the clearest evidence that the -where words straddle two categories.
entries.agreement: no agreement of its own, but fronting it forces subject-auxiliary inversion — Nowhere is this clearer than in the third chapter, ✗ Nowhere this is clearer. This is a genuine rule, not a stylistic option, and it applies to every fronted negative adverb.
entries.pattern: [positive verb] nowhere (The path led nowhere) · Nowhere + [auxiliary] + [subject] + [verb] (fronted, with inversion) · nowhere to [verb] (nowhere to sit) · nowhere near [noun/adjective] · out of nowhere · the middle of nowhere · get nowhere · nowhere else
entries.contrast: Against not … anywhere, the same meaning with different weight and different available positions: We got nowhere and We didn't get anywhere are both standard, but only nowhere can be fronted, and fronting it triggers inversion. The one-negative rule applies as it does across this whole file: ✗ We didn't get nowhere is negative concord, nonstandard in edited American English. Nowhere near is a fixed degree phrase meaning far from — nowhere near enough money — and is not about location at all. And nowheres with an -s is regional and nonstandard; see nowheres, anywheres, somewheres.
entries.see also: somewhere, anywhere, everywhere, nothing, nowheres, anywheres, somewheres

entries.meaning: The American colloquial parallel series to somewhere, anywhere, everywhere, and nowhere. They arose in nineteenth-century American English and remain a recognizable marker of it; their meanings and their polarity are identical to the -where forms, and only the idioms fail to transfer.
examples: Let's go someplace quiet and talk it through.
I couldn't find parking anyplace near the arena.
She's got relatives everyplace between Tulsa and Amarillo.
There was noplace to sit, so we ate standing up.
Take it someplace else — this counter is closed.
Is there anyplace around here that's open past nine?
entries.pronunciation note: each keeps the stress pattern of its -where twin, with a full secondary stress on -place; the /s/ is voiceless, never /z/. All four are written solid in American English, though some place as two words is also seen and means the same thing
entries.русский: разг. амер.: где-то, где-нибудь, везде, нигде — просторечные замены форм на -where
entries.case: none — adverbs take no case
entries.register: informal American English. Someplace and anyplace are common in speech and in relaxed writing; everyplace and noplace are rarer and read as more markedly casual. All four sound distinctly American to British ears, and a formal American editor will usually restore the -where form
entries.type: compound indefinite adverbs, American colloquial variants of the -where forms
entries.person / number: invariant.
entries.refers to: a place, exactly as the corresponding -where word does, with the same polarity behavior: someplace asserts, anyplace questions and denies, everyplace universalizes, noplace negates.
entries.agreement: no agreement of their own. Noplace fronted takes inversion just as nowhere does, though the fronted construction is stiff enough that it is rarely paired with these informal forms.
entries.pattern: [verb] someplace / anyplace / everyplace / noplace · someplace [adjective] (someplace warm) · someplace / anyplace else · [negated verb] anyplace · anyplace [clause] (anyplace they'll take a check)
entries.contrast: These are stylistic variants, not different words: let's go someplace quiet and let's go somewhere quiet are identical in meaning, and only register separates them. The -place forms are one notch more casual, and noplace and everyplace are two. They do not take the fixed idioms that nowhere owns — ✗ out of noplace, ✗ the middle of noplace, ✗ noplace near enough are all wrong, because those phrases are frozen with nowhere. That is the practical rule: use the -place forms for ordinary reference to location, and keep the -where forms for every idiom.
entries.see also: somewhere, anywhere, everywhere, nowhere

entries.meaning: Points at a place that exists but is unspecified. Two uses.
examples: I left my keys somewhere in this house. — sense 1
Let's find somewhere quiet to sit. — sense 1, adjective following
We need somewhere to park before the game lets out. — sense 1
The estimate came in somewhere around eight thousand. — sense 2
It happened somewhere between Flagstaff and the state line. — sense 2
Now we're getting somewhere.

senses.head: An unidentified place
body: I left my keys somewhere in this house. Takes the family's usual postmodifiers: somewhere quiet, somewhere to park, somewhere I've never been.

senses.head: An approximator
body: Before a number or a range it hedges: somewhere around forty dollars, somewhere between March and May.
examples: I left my keys somewhere in this house. — sense 1
Let's find somewhere quiet to sit. — sense 1, adjective following
We need somewhere to park before the game lets out. — sense 1
The estimate came in somewhere around eight thousand. — sense 2
It happened somewhere between Flagstaff and the state line. — sense 2
Now we're getting somewhere.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on some-; -where keeps a full /ɛr/ and a secondary stress and never reduces. Many Americans have a slight /hw/ at the start of -where, chiefly in the South and among older speakers; most say plain /w/
entries.русский: где-то, куда-то — неназванное место; также «примерно» (somewhere around fifty)
entries.case: none — adverbs take no case
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: compound indefinite adverb (assertive) — not a pronoun
entries.person / number: invariant.
entries.refers to: a place, location, or destination that exists but is unidentified. In the approximator use (somewhere around fifty) it refers to a point on a numerical range.
entries.agreement: no agreement of its own. After a preposition it can head what looks like a noun phrase — from somewhere in Ohio, in somewhere warm — which is why its category is genuinely mixed.
entries.pattern: [verb] somewhere · somewhere [adjective] — the adjective follows (somewhere quiet) · somewhere to [verb] (somewhere to park) · [preposition] somewhere (from somewhere, in somewhere warm) · somewhere else · somewhere around / between [number]
entries.contrast: Polarity as elsewhere in this file: somewhere in plain statements, anywhere under a negative, in a question, or after if — with the offer exception intact, so Shall we go somewhere for lunch? is an invitation while Shall we go anywhere for lunch? is not English at all in that reading. Against the pronoun something, the difference is what slot they fill: something quiet is a thing, somewhere quiet is a place, and only something can be a direct object (I bought something, ✗ I bought somewhere). The idiom getting somewhere means making progress and is the positive counterpart of getting nowhere.
entries.see also: anywhere, everywhere, nowhere, something, someplace, anyplace, everyplace, noplace

entries.meaning: The unprintable end of the minimizer family: three ways of saying nothing at all as rudely as American English says it. They earn an entry because a learner meets them constantly in film, in sports talk, and in argument, and needs to know two things at once — that they are ordinary in that register, and that they are unusable in every other.
examples: He's been on the job a month and knows dick about the hydraulics. — positive verb, negative meaning
Two weeks of overtime and I got shit for it.
That warranty isn't worth shit once you break the seal. — under a negative, and the meaning is unchanged
— What did the inspector turn up? — Dick. — standing alone as an answer, which is where these words are strongest
They did fuck all about the leak until the ceiling came down. — the British-flavored member of the set
Never in: a classroom, an interview, a customer call, or anything with an editor in front of it.
Formal rewrite: The inspection produced no findings. — what goes in the report where the spoken version had dick
entries.pronunciation note: one syllable each except fuck all, which takes its main stress on all and runs the /k/ straight into the vowel with no release between them, [ˌfʌk ˈɔl]; merged speakers have /ɑl/. The final /t/ of shit is an unreleased or glottal stop before a pause, [ʃɪʔ], and a tap before a vowel. These words have no weak form. They exist to carry the nuclear stress of the clause, so everything around them reduces instead: he doesn't know dick about it runs [i ˈdʌzn̩ ˈnoʊ ˈdɪk əˈbaʊɾ ɪt], with he at its weak /i/ and the /t/ of about tapped
entries.русский: груб.: ни хера, ни хрена; fuck all — ни хуя — «совсем ничего»
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object, and no genitive (✗ dick's)
entries.register: vulgar. Dick and shit in this use are obscene in most American settings and are bleeped on broadcast television; fuck all is the strongest of the three, is chiefly British and Irish, and reaches American speech mainly through imported film and television and in the fixed sweet fuck all. Never in a classroom, a job interview, a customer call, a cover letter, or any edited prose that is not quoting somebody — the printable substitutes are squat and diddly-squat one notch up, zilch and zip two notches up, and plain nothing in writing
entries.type: minimizer indefinite pronouns (negative) — vulgar
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no plural and no gender.
entries.refers to: nothing at all — knowledge, effort, money, help, or results, and most often somebody else's competence. Non-human referents only; for a person use nobody. The pronoun shit is a mass quantity word and has nothing to do with the countable noun of a shit or the plural of the shits.
entries.agreement: singular verb in the uncommon subject use — Dick is what we got for two weeks of overtime. Their ordinary home is the object slot, where they trigger no agreement at all. As with every minimizer, the verb may be negative or positive with no change in meaning: he knows dick about engines and he doesn't know dick about engines both say he knows nothing.
entries.pattern: [negated verb] dick / shit / fuck all (You don't know dick) · [positive verb] dick (He knows dick about it) · not worth shit · know dick about [noun] · do fuck all · sweet fuck all (the intensified British form) · dick standing alone as an answer (What did they find? — Dick.)
entries.contrast: These are jack and squat with the euphemism stripped off, and they behave identically. All of them are negative-polarity minimizers whose bare form already means nothing, so the negative on the verb is optional and changes nothing: I got shit for it and I didn't get shit for it are the same complaint, and neither is a double negative. Against zilch, nada, bupkis, zip, which run the other way and refuse a negated verb (✓ I got zilch, ✗ I didn't get zilch). Against jack, register is the only difference: jack is the clipped euphemism that passes in ordinary conversation, and these three are the words the euphemism was invented to avoid. Two homograph traps, both live. The ordinary noun shit is everywhere in idiom (give a shit, the shit hit the fan, a load of shit) and is not this pronoun; and the article reverses the meaning — that record is the shit is high praise in American slang, where that record is shit is the opposite. Dick is also the man's name, the noun for a detective in older writing, and an insult for a person (he's a dick), none of which is the pronoun.
entries.variants: jack shit, jack squat, jack diddly (the blends), sweet fuck all, bugger all, sod all (all three chiefly British and Irish), not a damn thing, squat, diddly-squat, zilch (the printable equivalents)
entries.see also: jack, jack shit, diddly, diddly-squat, squat, zilch, nada, bupkis, zip, nothing, none, nobody, nothing (negative concord)

entries.meaning: Says nothing with force and an American accent. All three are minimizers: they name the smallest conceivable quantity in order to deny even that much, which is why they live in complaints — about how much somebody knows, how much they did, and how much they were paid. Diddly-squat is the full form, squat the clipping, and diddly the mildest survivor of a chain of euphemisms that began well below the belt.
examples: He's been on the job three weeks and knows squat about the wiring. — positive verb, negative meaning
We sat in that meeting for two hours and got diddly-squat out of it.
That extended warranty isn't worth diddly. — under a negative, and the meaning is unchanged
— How much did the settlement come to? — Squat. — standing alone as an answer, which is where these words are strongest
The new filter didn't do diddly-squat for the noise in the ductwork.
She knows squat about football and picked the bracket anyway.
Formal rewrite: The revised policy produced no measurable change. — what an editor puts where didn't do squat was
entries.pronunciation note: main stress falls on squat, whose vowel is that of cot; the final /t/ is regularly an unreleased stop or a glottal stop before a pause, [ˈskwɑʔ], and a tap before a vowel, so squat about it runs [ˈskwɑɾ əˈbaʊɾ ɪt]. These words have no weak form. They exist to carry the nuclear stress of the clause, so they never reduce; what reduces is everything around them, which is why he doesn't know squat about it comes out [i ˈdʌzn̩ ˈnoʊ ˈskwɑɾ əˈbaʊɾ ɪt], with he at its weak /i/. The older doodly-squat /ˈdudli ˌskwɑt/ is still heard in the South
entries.русский: разг., грубовато: ни фига, ни шиша, ноль — «совсем ничего»; мягче, чем dick и jack shit
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object, and no genitive (✗ squat's)
entries.register: informal. Diddly is the mildest and the most dated, diddly-squat is the everyday full form, and bare squat is the commonest and the bluntest. All three are generally traced to doodly-squat, where squat is a euphemism for excrement, so they are mildly coarse rather than clean; none of them survives an editor, and formal prose uses nothing
entries.type: minimizer indefinite pronoun (negative)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no plural and no gender.
entries.refers to: nothing at all, or the smallest imaginable amount of something — knowledge, effort, money, or results. Non-human referents only; for a person use nobody. Back-reference is it, though in practice these words sit at the end of the clause and are rarely referred back to at all.
entries.agreement: singular verb in the uncommon subject use — Diddly-squat has changed since the audit. Their ordinary home is the object slot, where they trigger no agreement. The one fact to memorize is that the verb may be negative or positive with no change in meaning: he knows squat about engines and he doesn't know squat about engines both say he knows nothing.
entries.pattern: [negated verb] squat / diddly / diddly-squat (I didn't get squat) · [positive verb] squat (I got squat) · not worth diddly-squat · know squat about [noun] · do squat · squat standing alone as an answer (How much did they pay? — Squat.)
entries.contrast: The polarity of this little family is genuinely odd and is the whole reason it needs an entry. Squat patterns like a negative-polarity item, loving a negated verb exactly as anything does — but unlike anything it also works after a positive verb and stays negative. ✗ I know anything about it is not English in that meaning, while ✓ I know squat about it means I know nothing about it. So I didn't get squat and I got squat both say the speaker got nothing, and neither is a double negative. That behavior belongs to minimizers generally — I didn't sleep a wink, he didn't lift a finger — and it is why this group sits at the edge of the no- series rather than inside it. Against zilch, nada, bupkis, zip, which mean the same thing and go the other way: ✓ I got zilch, ✗ I didn't get zilch. Against nothing, identical in meaning and nowhere near it in register. And keep the pronoun apart from its homographs: squat is also a verb (squat down) and a countable noun (a deep squat, a squat in an empty building), and only the pronoun means nothing.
entries.variants: doodly-squat (the older Southern form), diddly-poo, jack squat, jack diddly — all interchangeable, all informal, and all products of the same euphemism treadmill
entries.see also: jack, jack shit, zilch, nada, bupkis, zip, nothing, none, nobody, anything, nothing (negative concord), dick, shit, fuck all

entries.term: God knows what, God knows who
entries.meaning: A frozen clause that stopped being about God and became a pro-form: it fills the slot where the name of a thing or a person would go and then declares the slot unfillable. What it adds to the plain indefinites is an attitude — exasperation, suspicion, or a flat refusal to guess.
examples: He keeps God knows what in that storage unit.
She was on the phone with God knows who until two in the morning.
God knows what is living under that back porch. — the subject slot, with a singular verb
The box had screws, dead batteries, and God knows what else in it. — closing a list
Heaven knows what the neighbors made of all that. — the minced variant, no less common in America than the original
— Who signed for the delivery? — God knows. — the bare phrase, standing alone as an answer
Compare the ordinary clause: God knows what he was thinking, and He isn't telling. — a pause and a falling tone after knows, and a genuine claim about who knows what
entries.pronunciation note: spoken as one unit, with the main stress on the wh- word, a secondary stress on God, and knows sitting in the trough between them with no stress of its own. The reduction is on the middle: the /d/ of God is regularly unreleased or lost before the /n/ of knows, giving the everyday [ˌɡɑ noʊz ˈwʌt]. Southern and older speakers may keep an initial /hw/ on what. Say it with a pause and a fall after knows and it stops being this pronoun
entries.русский: бог знает что, бог знает кто — с оттенком раздражения или подозрения
entries.case: none — invariant; no genitive
entries.register: informal to neutral, and mildly profane for a good many American speakers, which is exactly why the minced variants exist. Heaven knows and goodness knows are the mild ones, Lord knows is the warm and chiefly Southern one, and God knows is the one that will not be said in front of some grandmothers. An editor replaces the whole phrase with a fact
entries.type: fused indefinite pro-form — a frozen clause standing in a noun-phrase slot
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant. Inside the phrase, knows is frozen in the third-person singular present: ✗ God knew what, ✗ God know what.
entries.refers to: a thing (what) or a person (who) that the speaker cannot identify and assumes nobody else can either — with parallel forms for place, time, reason, and manner (God knows where, God knows when, God knows why, God knows how). What separates it from the plain indefinites is attitude: it does not merely decline to name the referent, it declares the naming hopeless, usually with exasperation or suspicion attached.
entries.agreement: singular verb when the phrase is the subject — God knows what is living under that porch, God knows who has a key to this door. In the object slot it triggers no agreement at all, which is where it spends most of its life.
entries.pattern: [verb] God knows what (He keeps God knows what in there) · [preposition] God knows who · God knows what [singular verb] · and God knows what else (closing a list) · God knows where / when / why / how (the parallel forms) · God only knows (the intensified bare form) · God knows standing alone as an answer
entries.contrast: The trap is that the same words are also an ordinary clause with an ordinary meaning, and intonation is what separates them: God knows what he was thinking run together with the peak on what is the pro-form and means nobody has any idea, while God knows with its own falling contour and a pause after it is a claim about God's knowledge and the speaker's ignorance (God knows, I don't). Against something and something or other: those leave the referent unidentified, where this one insists it is unidentifiable and adds a shrug of disapproval. Against whatchamacallit, which is a name the speaker has mislaid, and you-know-what, which is a name the speaker has and will not say. One boundary worth marking: put a noun straight after it — God knows what address, God knows how many forms — and the phrase is working as a determiner on that noun rather than filling the slot by itself; the pronoun use is the one that stands alone.
entries.variants: heaven knows what, Lord knows what, goodness knows what, God only knows what, who knows what, God knows who / where / when / why / how, God knows what else
entries.see also: something, something or other, whatchamacallit, thingamajig, whatsit, you-know-who, you-know-what, so-and-so, whatnot, who cares, who knows

entries.meaning: Denies that any knowledge, effort, or benefit exists, in the bluntest terms the language keeps in ordinary circulation. Its normal subject is somebody else's competence, and its normal home is an argument.
examples: You don't know jack about running a kitchen at capacity.
Two years of physical therapy and it did jack shit for the pain. — vulgar, and exactly the register the speaker intends
They promised us overtime and delivered jack.
— What did the inspector find? — Jack. — standing alone as an answer
That coupon is worth jack on a sale item.
He hasn't done jack squat since the transfer went through. — the blended euphemism, printable where the original is not
Formal rewrite: The course of therapy produced no improvement.
entries.pronunciation note: main stress on shit in the two-word form, with the /k/ running straight into the /ʃ/ and no release between them, [ˌdʒæk ˈʃɪt]. No weak form — like the rest of the minimizers these words take the nuclear stress of the clause and never reduce, while the frame around them does, so he doesn't know jack about it runs [i ˈdʌzn̩ ˈnoʊ ˈdʒæk əˈbaʊɾ ɪt] with he at /i/ and the /t/ of about tapped
entries.русский: разг. ни фига (jack); груб. ни хера (jack shit) — «совсем ничего»
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; no genitive
entries.register: informal, and vulgar in the full form. Jack shit is bleeped on broadcast television and cut from any published prose that is not quoting speech. Bare jack is the clipped euphemism and passes in ordinary conversation, in sports talk, and in workplace complaint, though not in writing that has an editor. Jack shit is recorded in American English from the mid-twentieth century and jack is the clipping of it, which is why jack still carries a whiff of the longer phrase for many listeners
entries.type: minimizer indefinite pronoun (negative)
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no plural and no gender.
entries.refers to: nothing at all — knowledge, effort, money, or help. Non-human referents only. It has nothing to do with the personal name Jack, and nothing to do with the jack of every man jack of them, which means the opposite.
entries.agreement: singular verb in the rare subject use; normally the object of a verb, where it triggers no agreement at all. As with the rest of the minimizers, a negated verb and a positive verb give the same reading: he knows jack and he doesn't know jack both say he knows nothing.
entries.pattern: [negated verb] jack / jack shit (You don't know jack) · [positive verb] jack (He knows jack about it) · not worth jack · know jack about [noun] · do jack shit · jack squat / jack diddly (the blended euphemisms) · jack standing alone as an answer
entries.contrast: Grammatically identical to diddly, diddly-squat, squat — same minimizer polarity, so the negated verb is optional and changes nothing — and one clear notch cruder in the full form. Against zilch, nada, bupkis, zip, which refuse the negated verb entirely. Against nothing, which is what all of them mean and what all of them are replaced by in edited prose. The homographs are the real hazard for a learner, because jack is one of the busiest words in American English: the tool (a car jack), the card (the jack of spades), the verb (jack up the price, and jacked for stolen), the socket (a headphone jack), the man's name, and the fixed every man jack of them meaning every single one. Only the pronoun means nothing, and it is identifiable by its position — object of a verb, usually with know, do, get, or be worth.
entries.variants: jack squat, jack diddly, jack all (chiefly British and Irish; American English uses bare jack), bugger all (British), squat and diddly-squat (the clean-mouthed equivalents)
entries.see also: diddly, diddly-squat, squat, zilch, nada, bupkis, zip, nothing, none, nobody, nothing (negative concord), dick, shit, fuck all

entries.meaning: Names the slot where a person's name goes and then leaves the slot empty, on purpose. It is the spoken equivalent of a blank line on a form, and it belongs to explanations rather than to narratives: nothing actually happened to so-and-so, because so-and-so is not anybody yet.
examples: Call so-and-so in payroll and ask for the reimbursement code.
The letter always reads the same: Mr. So-and-so agrees to pay by the first of the month.
He kept telling us so-and-so said this and so-and-so said that, and never once gave a name.
It is always so-and-so's turn to make the coffee, and it is never mine. — the genitive
You sign here, so-and-so countersigns there, and the clerk stamps it. — walking a listener through a procedure
That nosy old so-and-so has been reading our mail. — the insult noun, with an article in front of it
Compare such-and-such a date, where the blank is a date instead of a person. — a determiner, catalogued in the determiner dictionary
entries.pronunciation note: main stress on the first so, secondary on the second, and the middle word is and in its weak form only — /ən/, or a syllabic /n̩/ with no vowel of its own, never the full /ænd/. That is why the phrase is three words on the page and about two and a half beats in the mouth: [ˈsoʊ ən ˌsoʊ], often [ˈsoʊn̩ˌsoʊ]. The same obligatory weak and runs through such-and-such, cat-and-mouse, and bread-and-butter
entries.русский: такой-то, имярек — намеренно не названное лицо; бранное — «такой-сякой»
entries.case: none for the pronoun — one invariant form for subject and object; the genitive so-and-so's is formed freely
entries.register: neutral to informal in the placeholder sense. An American meets it wherever somebody is describing a procedure rather than an event — a supervisor explaining a workflow, a lawyer reading a form aloud. The insult sense is a minced oath, a polite stand-in for a word the speaker declines to use, and it reads as mild and a little old-fashioned
entries.type: placeholder indefinite pronoun (person); also a countable noun in the insult sense
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular. The pronoun is invariant; the insult noun takes an article and pluralizes (a nosy so-and-so, a pair of lazy so-and-sos), which the pronoun never does.
entries.refers to: a person the speaker deliberately leaves unnamed — either because the name is beside the point (call so-and-so in payroll and get the code) or because the speaker is reciting a form rather than a fact (Mr. So-and-so hereby agrees to pay). It never means a person the speaker is unable to identify: that is somebody. For a thing, a date, or an amount left blank in the same way, English uses such-and-such, which takes a noun after it and is therefore a determiner: see such-and-such (a).
entries.agreement: singular verb — So-and-so signs at the bottom and the clerk files it, So-and-so from the county was supposed to call. Back-reference is singular they when no gender is in view (so-and-so turns in their form), and he or she when the speaker has a particular person in mind and is withholding only the name.
entries.pattern: so-and-so [singular verb] · [verb] so-and-so · [preposition] so-and-so · Mr. / Mrs. / Ms. So-and-so (capitalized, in mock-formal citation) · so-and-so in [department] · so-and-so's [noun] · a [adjective] so-and-so (the insult noun) · such-and-such (the thing-and-date equivalent, a determiner)
entries.contrast: Four words divide this territory and they are not interchangeable. So-and-so is a blank nobody has filled in — no particular person has been chosen, or the speaker is deliberately not naming one. what's-his-name is a name the speaker once had and has lost, which is why it always points at a particular person both parties know. you-know-who is a name the speaker has and refuses to say out loud. And somebody is the genuinely indefinite one: it asserts that a person exists and claims no knowledge of who. Against such-and-such, the same construction in a different slot — such-and-such leans on a following noun through the article (such-and-such a date), so it is a determiner, while so-and-so stands alone and never modifies a noun: ✗ so-and-so a clerk. The insult use is a different word class entirely, with an article in front of it and a plural available.
entries.variants: so and so (open spelling, common and not an error), Mr. So-and-so, thus and so (dated), John Doe and Jane Doe (the legal and hospital placeholders), such-and-such (the determiner counterpart)
entries.see also: somebody, someone, something or other, what's-his-name, what's-her-name, what's-his-face, you-know-who, you-know-what, whatchamacallit, thingamajig, whatsit, such-and-such (a)

entries.meaning: Stands in for the name of an object while the speaker's memory is looking for it. The three headwords are interchangeable, and the choice among them and among the long list of synonyms is regional and generational rather than semantic — the word means that thing, you know the one, and it depends on the listener being able to see or infer which thing.
examples: Hand me the whatchamacallit — the little brass fitting on the end of the hose.
The thingamajig that holds the pump to the bracket has rusted through.
I've lost the whatsit that came with the blender and now it won't lock.
There are two thingamajigs in that drawer and I don't know what either one does. — the plural, which no true pronoun in this file can form
Somewhere in the toolbox there's a doohickey for exactly this. — the folksier synonym
She called it a whatchamacallit for a week before somebody told her it was a grommet.
Formal rewrite: the coupling at the end of the hose.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on the first syllable of each, and every syllable in the middle is a schwa, which is the whole point of the words: they are frozen weak forms. Whatchamacallit is the sentence what you may call it with you at its weak /jə/ — that is the -cha- — and may at /mə/; whatsit is what is it given the same treatment. Because the reduction is already baked into the spelling there is no further weak form; the words sound the same fast or slow. Cot-caught merged Americans have [ˈwʌtʃəməˌkɑlɪt], and Southern and older speakers may keep an initial /hw/ on the what- forms
entries.русский: разг.: штуковина, штука, как её там — предмет, название которого забылось
entries.case: none in the pronoun use; as nouns they take the ordinary genitive (the whatsit's cover)
entries.register: informal. Ordinary in speech and in relaxed writing everywhere in the country; an editor replaces them with the object's real name, or with the fitting, the part, the device
entries.type: placeholder pro-forms for a thing — informal; grammatically they behave as countable nouns at least as much as pronouns
entries.person / number: third person. Unlike every true pronoun in this file, they inflect for number: a whatchamacallit, two thingamajigs, those whatsits.
entries.refers to: a physical object whose name the speaker cannot retrieve at that moment — non-human, and nearly always something concrete enough to point at. For a person whose name has gone the same way, use what's-his-name; for a thing the speaker never meant to name in the first place, something or other.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the word itself, not with anything else: The whatchamacallit is stripped, Both thingamajigs are missing, Those whatsits were in the drawer. That is a real break from the twelve compounds, which are singular no matter what the meaning is.
entries.pattern: a / the / that + whatchamacallit (the article is normal, which no true pronoun allows) · whatchamacallit [verb agreeing in number] · [verb] the whatsit · the whatsit's [noun] · that whatchamacallit on the [noun] · thingamajigs (plural)
entries.contrast: Against something, the true pronoun: something takes no article and no plural (✓ something is stripped, ✗ a something is stripped), while these take both, which is the clearest evidence that they are placeholder nouns rather than pronouns proper. Against whatnot, which closes a list and can never be a subject or take an article. Against what's-his-name, which does this same job for people. The synonyms are worth sorting by flavor rather than by meaning, since the meaning is identical: doohickey and doodad are general American and read as folksy; thingamabob is jocular; thingummy and whatsit have a British ring, though whatsit is thoroughly at home in America; dingus is chiefly Upper Midwestern, from Dutch; gizmo began as mid-century military slang and has drifted toward meaning gadget rather than forgotten name; and widget has been captured by economics and software and no longer works as a placeholder in speech at all.
entries.variants: whatchacallit, whatsis, whatsitsname, thingamabob, thingummy, thingy, doohickey, doodad, dingus, gizmo
entries.see also: something, something or other, whatnot, what's-his-name, what's-her-name, what's-his-face, so-and-so, what have you, God knows what, God knows who

entries.ipa: /ˌwʌts ɪz ˈneɪm/, /ˌwʌts ɚ ˈneɪm/, /ˌwʌts ɪz ˈfeɪs/
entries.meaning: Points at a specific person and admits that the name has gone. It presumes shared knowledge, which is why it is nearly always followed by a repair clause — what's-his-name, the one who used to run the front desk — supplying by description what the speaker cannot supply by name.
examples: What's-his-name from the insurance office called again this morning.
I ran into what's-her-name at the hardware store — the one who used to run the front desk.
Ask what's-his-name in shipping; he'll know where the pallet went.
That's what's-his-name's truck blocking the loading ramp. — the genitive, ordinary in speech
Old what's-his-face still hasn't returned my extension ladder. — the dismissive member of the set
I introduced them to what's-their-name from the co-op, since I wasn't sure either way. — the gender-neutral form
Compare the ordinary question: What's his name? — full /h/, stress on name, and a genuine request for information
entries.pronunciation note: main stress on the last element, and the whole phrase is spoken as a single word. The weak forms are the entire story here. His appears only as /ɪz/ with the /h/ dropped, and her only as /ɚ/, which is why the running-together spellings whatsisname and whatsername look nothing like the words they are made of. Both weak forms are compulsory: put a full /hɪz/ or /hɚ/ back in and the phrase turns into the ordinary question What is his name? Southern and older speakers may keep an initial /hw/ on what's
entries.русский: разг.: как его там, как её там — знакомый человек, чьё имя забыто; -face пренебрежительно
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; the genitive what's-his-name's is clumsy on the page and perfectly ordinary in speech
entries.register: informal, with a dismissive edge that grows across the set. What's-his-name is plain forgetfulness; what's-his-face is openly dismissive and mildly rude about the person it names. Both are cut from edited prose, which supplies the name or writes a colleague, the contractor, the man from the county
entries.type: placeholder pro-form for a person whose name the speaker has forgotten
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular. This is the one corner of the indefinite system that marks gender, and it marks it on the pronoun buried inside the phrase: what's-his-name for a man, what's-her-name for a woman. A gender-neutral what's-their-name is built on the same model as singular they and is used when the speaker does not know the person's gender or does not wish to specify it; it is considerably less common than the two gendered forms, is not yet recorded in most American dictionaries, and inflects exactly as they do (what's-their-name's car).
entries.refers to: a particular person, known to both speaker and listener, whose name the speaker cannot retrieve. That is what separates this phrase from everything else in the file: it is definite in meaning and indefinite only in form. It cannot introduce a person the listener has never met, and it cannot refer to a thing — for a thing use whatchamacallit.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — What's-his-name is on the phone again, What's-her-name has already signed off on it. Back-reference follows the gender the form encodes (what's-her-name left her badge); with what's-their-name it is they.
entries.pattern: what's-his-name [singular verb] · [verb] what's-his-name · [preposition] what's-his-name · that guy — what's-his-name — from the county (parenthetical, its commonest home) · what's-his-name's [noun] · old what's-his-face
entries.contrast: Against so-and-so: so-and-so is a blank nobody has filled in, this is a blank that was filled in and has gone missing. Against you-know-who: that is a name the speaker has and declines to say. Against somebody: genuinely indefinite, with no particular person in view — somebody called reports an unknown caller, what's-his-name called reports a known one whose name will not come. Against the plain question What's his name?, which is a different structure altogether: the question stresses name and keeps a full /h/, the placeholder is one flat unit with /ɪz/ and no question intonation. And what's-his-face is about a face only historically — it means the same thing with more attitude.
entries.variants: whatshisname, whatsisname, whatsername (the run-together spellings), what's-her-face, what's-their-name (gender-neutral, newer and less common), whozit, whatshername
entries.see also: so-and-so, you-know-who, you-know-what, whatchamacallit, thingamajig, whatsit, somebody, someone, they (generic)

entries.meaning: Names a referent by pointing at the listener's knowledge of it instead of at the referent itself. The whole construction is a piece of social machinery: it says we both know who I mean, and I am not going to say it here, and the reason for the discretion is left to the listener.
examples: You-know-who has been asking about the schedule again. — said in front of the person's children
Don't leave you-know-what on the kitchen table where she'll see it.
I ran it past you-know-who before I sent it out. — discretion, not forgetfulness
That's you-know-who's car in the driveway, so keep your voice down. — the genitive
In the books he is never named; he is You-Know-Who. — the capitalized proper-noun use
He can take that memo and file it you-know-where. — the euphemism, standing in for a word the speaker will not say
Compare the ordinary clause: You know what? Let's just go. — a discourse opener, not a pronoun
entries.pronunciation note: main stress on the last element, with the whole phrase spoken as one unit and no pause inside it. The weak form sits on you, which reduces to /jə/ exactly as it does everywhere else in the language, giving [jə noʊ ˈhu]; know keeps its full /oʊ/ because it is carrying the middle of the phrase. An evenly stressed you know who with a rising tone is not this pronoun at all — it is the question You know who?
entries.русский: сам знаешь кто, сам знаешь что — то, что оба знают, но говорящий не называет вслух
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; the genitive you-know-who's is ordinary in speech
entries.register: informal and conspiratorial. It presumes shared knowledge and a reason for discretion — somebody in earshot, a child in the room, a subject the family does not discuss. Capitalized You-Know-Who is a proper-noun use, most famously the epithet for the villain of the Harry Potter books, which is where a good many young Americans meet the construction first
entries.type: placeholder pro-form for a referent the speaker declines to name
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no plural. You-know-who takes human referents; you-know-what takes non-human ones.
entries.refers to: a person, or a thing, whose identity both speaker and listener already know and which the speaker is deliberately not saying out loud. Like what's-his-name it is definite in meaning; unlike it, the name has not been forgotten but withheld.
entries.agreement: singular verb — You-know-who is asking about the schedule again, You-know-what has turned up in the garage. Back-reference follows the real referent's gender when both parties know it (you-know-who forgot her keys again), and it for you-know-what.
entries.pattern: you-know-who [singular verb] · [verb] you-know-who · [preposition] you-know-who · you-know-who's [noun] · a little you-know-what (the euphemism, standing in for a noun the speaker will not use) · You-Know-Who (capitalized, as a name)
entries.contrast: The trap is the plain clause you know what / you know who, which is a completely different structure and far commoner: You know what? I'm leaving is a discourse opener and You know who I saw? is a question, and neither is a pronoun. Intonation separates them in speech and the hyphens separate them in writing. Against what's-his-name, the difference is forgotten against withheld; against so-and-so, never-named against not-said-aloud; against somebody, genuinely unidentified against perfectly well identified. The euphemistic you-know-what also stands in for a word the speaker will not utter — he can take that memo and file it you-know-where — which is the same minced-oath move that gives so-and-so its insult sense, and you-know-where exists in that use only.
entries.variants: you-know-where (euphemistic only), you-know-when (rare), You-Know-Who (capitalized as a name), he-who-shall-not-be-named (jocular), a certain someone
entries.see also: so-and-so, what's-his-name, what's-her-name, what's-his-face, whatchamacallit, thingamajig, whatsit, somebody, something, what's what

entries.meaning: Closes an open-ended list by inviting the listener to extend it: whatever you can name belongs in the set. It is the most generous of the American list-closers and the only one that comes with a challenge attached, which is why it has been living on shop signs for a century.
examples: Sockets, wrenches, torque bars — you name it, it's in that chest.
She's done every job in the building: front desk, billing, scheduling, you name it.
They stock mufflers, brakes, alignment kits, you name it.
Rain, hail, a downed line — you name it — that trip went wrong every way a trip can.
You name it, and somebody in that family has broken it. — the fronted frame
Compare the live imperative: — Where do you want to eat? — You name it. — a full /ju/, its own contour, and a real invitation
Formal rewrite: tools of every description, or, in a contract, including but not limited to the items listed.
entries.pronunciation note: main stress on name, with the three words run together as a single unit and no pause anywhere inside it. The weak forms carry it: you reduces to /jə/ exactly as it does everywhere else in the language, and it to /ɪt/ with its /t/ tapped or glottalized into whatever follows, giving the everyday [jə ˈneɪm ɪʔ]. A full /ju/ with its own stress is not this pronoun at all — it is the live imperative You name it, meaning you choose
entries.русский: и что угодно, и всё такое прочее — закрывает открытый список: «чего там только нет»
entries.case: none — invariant
entries.register: informal. Ordinary in speech, in sales talk, and in advertising copy of every kind; edited prose replaces it with and so on or with a finished list, and technical, legal, and contractual writing needs including but not limited to instead
entries.type: frozen clause used as an indefinite pro-form; a list-closer
entries.person / number: second person in form and third person in reference; it has no number of its own, because it never governs a verb. Nothing inside it can move: ✗ you named it, ✗ he names it, ✗ you name them.
entries.refers to: any further item of the same kind, without limit — the open remainder of a list, things far more often than people. Its distinctive move is to hand the extending over to the listener: whatever you can think of is in the set.
entries.agreement: it takes no agreement of its own. When it closes a list that is the subject, the verb agrees with the list, not with the phrase: Hammers, saws, drills — you name it — are all on that wall. It is essentially never a subject by itself: ✗ You name it is in the drawer.
entries.pattern: [list] — you name it · [list], you name it · you name it, [clause] (You name it, we carry it) · it closes a list and never opens one, and it takes no question mark
entries.contrast: It belongs with whatnot and what have you, and it does one thing neither of them does: it hands the job to the listener. Whatnot says and more of the same; you name it says and anything else you care to think of, which is why it is the list-closer of the hardware store and the auto shop. It is also the only one of the three that can be fronted, in the fixed frame you name it, we've got it. Grammatically it is a fossil — an imperative with no imperative left in it — so it is invariant in every part. Against the live imperative it came from, which is a different sentence with a full /ju/, its own contour, and a real invitation: We can eat anywhere. You name it. And against the formal general extenders and so forth, and so on, and et cetera, which close a list without inviting anybody to extend it; those are quasi-coordinators rather than pronouns and are catalogued in the conjunction dictionary at and so forth and et cetera / etc..
entries.variants: you name it, we've got it (the fixed frame), whatever you can think of, and what have you, and whatnot, and everything
entries.see also: whatnot, what have you, anything, everything, something or other, and so forth

entries.meaning: Say nothing with emphasis, in the register of complaint, sports, and shop talk. All four are single-word negatives that need no negative verb to lean on, and their differences are entirely about flavor: zilch is neutral American slang, zip is the sportscaster's word, nada carries a shrug, and bupkis carries a punchline.
examples: We searched the whole attic and turned up zilch.
Three interviews and nada — not even a rejection email.
Twenty years at that company and he got bupkis when it folded.
They were up four to zip by the third inning. — the score use
— Any word back from the lab? — Zip. — standing alone as an answer
Her share of the settlement came to nada once the fees were taken out.
Formal rewrite: The search produced no results.
entries.pronunciation note: nada keeps the Spanish stress on the first syllable and the /ɑ/ of father, and its /d/ is a tap for most Americans, [ˈnɑɾə]; bupkis has first-syllable stress and a second vowel that wavers between /ə/ and /ɪ/. None of the four has a weak form — each is the word its sentence is built to land on, so it takes the nuclear stress and keeps a full vowel however fast the rest of the clause runs
entries.русский: разг., но не грубо: ноль, ничего, шиш, кот наплакал — «ничего совсем»
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object; no genitive
entries.register: informal but not coarse, which is what separates them from jack and squat: all four are printable, and zilch and zip turn up in American sports writing and in headlines. Zilch is generally traced to a character named Mr. Zilch in a humor magazine of the 1930s; zip for a score of zero is American and about a century old; nada is Spanish for nothing and has been in general American use since the middle of the twentieth century; bupkis is from Yiddish, literally beans by way of a Slavic root and often glossed as goat droppings, and it reached general American English through New York and through comedy writing, keeping a wry flavor the others do not have
entries.type: informal indefinite pronouns (negative), meaning nothing or zero
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant — no plural and no gender.
entries.refers to: nothing at all, zero — an amount, a result, a response, or a score. Non-human referents only. Zip and zilch are the two that serve as scores (we lost four to zip); nada and bupkis do not (✗ four to bupkis).
entries.agreement: singular verb when one of them is the subject, which is uncommon but perfectly grammatical — Zilch has come back from the lab, Nada is what we got for our trouble. Their usual place is the object or the complement, where they trigger no agreement at all.
entries.pattern: [positive verb] zilch / nada / bupkis / zip (We got zilch) · worth zilch · [number] to zip (a score) · zilch / zip standing alone as an answer · and I got bupkis for it · nada as a flat one-word reply
entries.contrast: All four mean what nothing means, with the register lowered and the volume raised, and the one grammatical fact to learn is that they carry the negation themselves and refuse a second one: ✓ I got zilch, while ✗ I didn't get zilch is a double negative that either reverses the sense or collapses into nonsense. That is exactly the opposite of squat and jack, which take a negated verb happily and mean the same with it or without it. Against nothing itself, interchangeable in meaning and never in register: a condolence note says nothing, a group chat says zilch. Against none, which needs a set already in view where these need none. And watch the homographs — zip is also the fastener, the verb (zip through), and the zip code; nada is a live Spanish word and stays Spanish inside a Spanish sentence.
entries.variants: bupkes, bubkes, bopkes (competing spellings of the Yiddish word), zippo, nix, goose egg (a zero, especially a score), nil (chiefly British, and in soccer scores), nada and zilch used adverbially in casual speech (it helped zilch)
entries.see also: nothing, none, diddly, diddly-squat, squat, jack, jack shit, naught, zero, dick, shit, fuck all

entries.meaning: A vernacular negative construction denying that any person satisfies the description, with the negation marked twice and the auxiliary fronted. It is the best-known example of English negative concord, and its wide circulation as a catchphrase has made it familiar to Americans who have never used it in their own speech.
examples: Ain't nobody home — nonstandard for Nobody is home.
Ain't nobody got time for that. — the catchphrase, from a 2012 local news interview
Ain't nobody gonna tell me how to run my own shop. — vernacular
Ain't nothing wrong with that truck. — the parallel -thing form
Standard rewrite: There isn't anybody home.
Standard rewrite: Nobody has time for that.
entries.pronunciation note: ain't is /eɪnt/; the /d/ of nobody taps, giving [ˈnoʊbəɾi]. In the fronted construction the whole phrase carries a single sweeping contour with the peak on no-
entries.русский: прост.: «никого нет», «никто и не...» — двойное отрицание с инверсией, вне нормы
entries.case: none — invariant
entries.register: vernacular. Rule-governed and completely systematic in African American English and in Southern and Appalachian vernacular English; stigmatized in edited American writing. It is also quoted constantly by speakers who do not otherwise use it, which is a separate fact about it
entries.type: negative-concord idiom with negative inversion — nonstandard in Standard American English
entries.person / number: third person, singular in form; the following verb takes the bare or -ing form.
entries.refers to: no person at all — human referents only, exactly as nobody does.
entries.agreement: the negated auxiliary ain't is invariant for person and number, and it precedes the subject. Ain't nobody home, Ain't nobody got time for that, Ain't nobody gonna tell me different.
entries.pattern: ain't nobody [adjective/locative] (Ain't nobody home) · ain't nobody [past participle / bare verb] (Ain't nobody got time) · ain't nobody gonna [verb] · ain't nothing / ain't no [noun] (the parallel forms)
entries.contrast: Two things happen at once here, and they are worth separating. Negative concord marks the negative twice, on the auxiliary and on the pronoun. Negative inversion moves the negated auxiliary in front of the subject. Crucially, the meaning is emphatic single negation — Ain't nobody home means nobody is home, not somebody is home. The old schoolroom claim that two negatives make a positive is a borrowing from logic and has never described how English actually works; what the doubled negative signals is emphasis, and what it signals socially is the speaker's variety. Standard equivalents: There isn't anybody home, Nobody is home, Nobody has time for that. Recognize it, read it, quote it accurately — and keep it out of a cover letter.
entries.see also: nobody, nothing (negative concord), nothing, ain't no, no (negative concord)

entries.meaning: An archaic pronoun meaning anything whatever. A modern American meets it in older literature, in legal boilerplate, and in the frozen hedge for aught I know, which means so far as I know with an added shrug.
examples: For aught I know, she never left the building that night. — the surviving idiom
If aught remains of the estate, it passes to the college. — archaic legal register
He would not take aught but what he had earned. — aught but = anything except
She was born in nineteen aught six. — the zero sense, from a misdivision of a naught
The album came out sometime in the aughts. — the decade, 2000 to 2009
Modern rewrite: For all I know, she never left the building.
entries.pronunciation note: one syllable, /ɔt/, a homophone of ought and — for the many Americans who merge cot and caught — of ot in otter without the -er. Merged speakers make aught and not rhyme exactly
entries.русский: устар., книжн.: что-либо, что-нибудь — живо лишь в обороте for aught I know «почём я знаю»
entries.case: none — invariant
entries.register: archaic and literary. In living American English it survives in one fixed phrase, for aught I know, and in the decade name the aughts
entries.type: archaic indefinite pronoun meaning anything
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant.
entries.refers to: anything at all — non-human referents. It is the historical ancestor of the nonassertive anything and appears in the same environments: negatives, questions, and conditionals.
entries.agreement: singular verb — If aught remains of the estate, it goes to the college.
entries.pattern: for aught I know (the surviving idiom) · if aught [singular verb] · [negated verb] aught · aught but [noun] (= anything except)
entries.contrast: Aught means anything; naught means nothing. They differ by one letter, they are opposites, and confusing them reverses a sentence, which is the main reason both are now avoided. The zero sense muddies matters further: the aughts for the decade beginning in 2000, and a nineteen-aught-six model, come from misdividing a naught as an aught, so historically the zero belongs to naught and aught acquired it by accident. The spelling ought for this word exists in older texts and is now avoided because of the modal verb.
entries.see also: naught, anything, nothing

entries.meaning: An archaic pronoun meaning nothing, worn down from Old English nā wiht, no thing. It survives chiefly in a few fixed phrases about wasted effort, and secondarily as a name for the digit zero — the noughts and crosses of the British game Americans call tic-tac-toe, spelled with the British nought.
examples: Two years of negotiation came to naught. — the living idiom
All that overtime was for naught once the contract fell through.
He set at naught every warning the inspector gave him. — formal and archaic
They had naught but a tent and a week of rations. — naught but = nothing but
The British write nought and say it for zero; Americans write naught and say zero.
Common error: ✗ all for not. The word is naught.
entries.pronunciation note: one syllable; for the many Americans who merge cot and caught it is a perfect homophone of not, which is exactly what it descends from. Unmerged speakers keep /ɔ/ in naught against /ɑ/ in not
entries.русский: устар., книжн.: ничто, ничего; как существительное — ноль (цифра)
entries.case: none — invariant
entries.register: archaic and literary, surviving in a handful of set phrases that are still in ordinary use: come to naught, all for naught, set at naught
entries.type: archaic indefinite pronoun meaning nothing; also a noun meaning zero
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular, invariant.
entries.refers to: nothing at all — non-human referents; and, as a noun, the digit zero.
entries.agreement: singular verb — All his planning came to naught.
entries.pattern: come to naught · all for naught · for naught · set at naught [noun] (= treat as worthless) · naught but [noun] (= nothing but) · avail naught / profit naught (archaic, verb + object)
entries.spelling: naught is the American form and nought the British, and British English additionally uses nought for the digit zero (nought point five), where Americans say zero or oh. Do not write ✗ all for not — the homophony with not makes this a common error, and it destroys the phrase. The living American descendant of the word is simply nothing, which is what a modern rewrite uses.
entries.contrast: Naught is nothing; aught is anything.
entries.see also: aught, nothing, none

entries.meaning: A single emphatic negation marked twice — on the auxiliary and again on the pronoun. Chaucer used it, Shakespeare used it, and it remains standard in French and Spanish; English lost it from the prestige dialect during the eighteenth century and it survives vigorously below that line. Learn to read it and never to write it in edited prose.
examples: I didn't see nothing. — nonstandard; standard: I didn't see anything or I saw nothing.
He don't know nothing about engines. — nonstandard twice: concord plus the verb form.
We couldn't find nobody who'd take the job. — nonstandard; standard: couldn't find anybody.
I can't get no satisfaction. — the best-known line in the construction, and unambiguous.
That's not nothing. — standard litotes: two negatives, deliberate, meaning it is significant.
I didn't say nothing was wrong. — standard: the negatives are in separate clauses.
entries.pronunciation note: identical to standard nothing — /ˈnʌθɪŋ/, casually [ˈnʌθɪn] or [ˈnʌʔn̩]. Nothing about the pronunciation marks the construction; the syntax does
entries.русский: ничего при отрицательном глаголе — двойное отрицание: в русском норма, в англ. нет
entries.case: none — invariant
entries.register: nonstandard in edited American English; systematic and rule-governed in African American English, in Southern and Appalachian vernacular, and in many other varieties worldwide. It is a reliable social marker, which is the whole reason to be able to recognize it
entries.type: compound indefinite pronoun in a clause that is already negated — nonstandard in Standard American English
entries.person / number: third person, grammatically singular — the agreement is entirely regular; what is nonstandard is the second negative, not the number.
entries.refers to: no thing at all — the meaning is a single emphatic negative, not a positive. I didn't see nothing means I saw nothing, never I saw something.
entries.agreement: singular verb, as always. The construction changes nothing about agreement: He don't know nothing is nonstandard twice over — once for the concord and once for the third-person -s — but He doesn't know nothing is nonstandard only for the concord.
entries.pattern: [negated verb] nothing (I didn't see nothing) · [negated verb] nobody / nowhere / no one (the parallel forms) · can't … no [noun] (can't get no satisfaction) · ain't nobody / ain't nothing (with negative inversion)
entries.contrast: Standard American English allows one negative marker per clause. There are therefore exactly two repairs, and they are not stylistic variants of each other: move the negative onto the verb and switch the pronoun to any- — I didn't see anything — or leave the negative on the pronoun and un-negate the verb — I saw nothing, which is heavier. Two superficially similar patterns are entirely standard and should not be confused with this one. Litotes doubles the negative on purpose to produce a positive: That's not nothing, the reaction was not uncommon. And negation across a clause boundary puts the two negatives in different clauses, where they never interact: I didn't say nothing was wrong is perfectly grammatical and means I did not say that nothing was wrong. The claim that two negatives make a positive is imported from logic; in English the second negative is agreement, not arithmetic, which is why I can't get no satisfaction has never once been misread.
entries.see also: nothing, nobody, ain't nobody, anything, no (negative concord)

entries.meaning: Regional and nonstandard variants of nowhere, anywhere, and somewhere, formed with a surviving adverbial -s. They are worth knowing because they are common in reported speech and in American literary dialect, and because a learner who meets them in Huckleberry Finn should not conclude that the standard forms take an -s.
examples: He wasn't nowheres to be found. — nonstandard; standard: nowhere to be found.
I ain't going nowheres tonight. — nonstandard, with negative concord on top.
She left it somewheres in the barn. — nonstandard; standard: somewhere.
It wasn't nowheres near enough. — nonstandard; standard: nowhere near.
Did you look anywheres besides the garage? — nonstandard; standard: anywhere.
Compare the standard survivals of the same ending: always, besides, nowadays, unawares.
entries.pronunciation note: identical to the standard forms with a final /z/ added; the /z/ is voiced because it follows a vowel-like /r/. Stress is unchanged
entries.русский: диал., прост.: нигде, где-нибудь, где-то — южные и сельские формы с лишним -s
entries.case: none in the modern sense; the -s is a fossilized genitive ending, not a plural
entries.register: nonstandard and regional. Heard in Southern and Midland American speech, in older rural New England, and in nineteenth-century literary dialect — Twain writes it constantly. Marked as an error by every American style guide
entries.type: compound indefinite adverbs with an adverbial genitive -s — nonstandard and regional
entries.person / number: invariant.
entries.refers to: a place, with exactly the meanings of the standard forms; the -s adds nothing but a regional flavor.
entries.agreement: no agreement of their own, as adverbs.
entries.pattern: [negated verb] nowheres / anywheres · [verb] somewheres · nowheres near [noun] · standard rewrite: drop the -s
entries.contrast: The -s is not random. It is the old adverbial genitive, the same ending that survives perfectly standardly in always, besides, nowadays, and unawares — and, as an optional extra, in afterwards and towards, where American English generally prefers the -s-less afterward and toward and both forms are standard. English simply stopped extending it, and the varieties that kept extending it to nowheres, anywheres, and somewheres are now marked. The related anyways sits one notch higher — still informal and still cut by editors, but far more widely used than the -where forms, and anyway is the form to write. Recognize these in dialogue and in Twain; drop the -s everywhere else.
entries.see also: nowhere, anywhere, somewhere, nothing (negative concord)

entries.meaning: Stands in for the unnamed remainder of a list, signaling that the speaker could go on and does not intend to. It is a coordination-closer rather than a true pronoun, which is why it is catalogued at the edge of this family rather than in its center. --- ← The grammar of pronouns · All categories
examples: The drawer's full of tape, twine, batteries, and whatnot.
She handles scheduling, invoicing, and whatnot for the whole practice.
We spent the weekend raking, hauling brush, and whatnot.
Bring a jacket, boots, and whatnot — it gets cold on the water.
He does contracts and licensing and what have you. — the near-synonym
There's an old whatnot in the front room with her grandmother's figurines. — the unrelated noun
entries.pronunciation note: stress on what; the /t/ of what is a tap or a glottal stop before the second element, giving [ˈwʌɾˌnɑt] or [ˈwʌʔˌnɑt]. Some Americans, chiefly Southern and older, keep an initial /hw/
entries.русский: разг.: и всякое такое, и тому подобное — только в конце перечисления
entries.case: none — invariant
entries.register: informal. Fine in speech and in relaxed writing, cut by editors in anything formal, where and so on or a complete list replaces it
entries.type: indefinite pro-form used only at the end of a list; informal
entries.person / number: third person; invariant. It has no number of its own because it never governs a verb.
entries.refers to: further unspecified items of the same kind as those already listed — usually things, occasionally activities. It cannot refer to a specific person.
entries.agreement: it takes no verb agreement, because it lives at the tail of a coordination and is essentially never a subject. ✗ Whatnot is in the drawer is not English; the tape and the string and whatnot are in the drawer takes its plural from the whole list.
entries.pattern: [item], [item], and whatnot · [item] and whatnot · and what have you (the near-synonym) · a whatnot (the unrelated noun: a small display shelf)
entries.contrast: And whatnot closes a list; it cannot open one, stand alone as a subject, or replace a single named item — ✗ Whatnot happened at the meeting is impossible, where something happened is fine. Its close relatives are and what have you, and all that, and stuff, and things like that, and the formal and so forth, et cetera. Do not confuse it with the homograph a whatnot, a countable noun naming a small many-shelved stand for ornaments, which pluralizes (two whatnots in the parlor) — the pro-form never takes an article and never pluralizes. Compare the determiner suchlike.
entries.see also: something or other, something, anything, whatchamacallit, thingamajig, whatsit, suchlike, you name it
